description: Weekly digest of trending tech blog articles

top_articles.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
top_articles.summary: Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android checkouts to <8s and builds to ~2m.

top_articles.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
top_articles.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

top_articles.title: How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI
top_articles.summary: When building a custom enterprise UI on top of Gemini Enterprise's :streamAssist API, developers must manually implement three core authentication layers. These include authenticating users or workloads via Google Identity or Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, managing third-party 3-legged OAuth (3LO) for Federated Connectors through the Keystore, and configuring on-demand per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents using Vertex AI Agent Engine and GCP Auth Manager.

top_articles.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
top_articles.summary: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning capabilities to a fast, efficient model built specifically for robotics. To help developers put these capabilities to work, the new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity transforms the platform into a comprehensive workbench supporting rapid hardware bring-up, MuJoCo simulation, and closed-loop control. Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

top_articles.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio
top_articles.summary: Developers can now build applications powered by Google Maps Platform directly within Google AI Studio by prompting Gemini with real-world geospatial concepts. The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. This setup grants developers immediate access to core APIs—including Maps, Places, and Routes—supported by daily sandbox quotas for seamless prototyping.

top_articles.title: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide
top_articles.summary: The newly launched AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide provides hardware-grounded design rules to help developers maximize performance on TPUs for LLMs and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) workloads. Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

top_articles.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
top_articles.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

top_articles.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
top_articles.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

top_articles.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
top_articles.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

top_articles.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
top_articles.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

Frontend.title: 问答是扁平的：先发布，再让模型看见
Frontend.summary:
前两篇都假设库里已经有「已上线」的问答。这一篇写它们怎么进来，以及答复怎样才算有依据。

第一篇把证据放在知识旁边：一条事实要能指回原文。这里没有再做一层向量检索去「找回证据」。一条问答的答案就是它自己的证据。编号是地址，正文是引用。

草稿看不见，发布才算数

导入或新建的问答先是草稿。问答页只读已上线的条目。星河这本现在是草稿 0、已上线 35。没点「正式发布」之前，问同样的问题会像库是空的。

一条问答可以单独改。下面是礼品那条：单次每人不超过 2000 新台币，不能造成义务或利益冲突，禁止现金、现金等价物。状态选已上线，保存之后才会进入勾选。

整本手册不是一条条手敲的。批量导入认这种文本：

Q1：工资一般什么时候发到账？
A1：工资按月发放，一般次月 5 个自然日内发放；遇银行假日，提前至前一个工作日发放。

问题和答案都可以跨行，一直写到下一题。导入进去仍是草稿，要点「正式发布」才进问答。

旧的「### Q1」加「答：」也能解析。给外部模型整理材料时，提示要求它按 Q数字 / A数字 输出。整理结果和导入器读的是同一种文本。早期有一次用了另一套标题格式，解析结果是 0 行，库是空的，问答就一律拒答。格式对齐之后，这个问题才消失。

六本库的条数在列表里就能看见，已上线的才会被勾选读到。

提示必须和程序发出去的 JSON 一致

勾选那一次，程序放进用户消息的字段是 question、document_title、entries、enumerative_query、composite_query、max_picks。每条 entry 只有编号、标题、摘要。没有「这是第几批」，也没有「请返回 done」。

提示如果还在说「父章节」「叶子」「后面还有几批」，模型会按一个不存在的目录作答。我们把这些句子从给模型的提示里拿掉了。分批是程序的事，模型只对眼前这份列表负责。

多件事的问题另有一段补充：每一件事都要有一条对得上的问答，不要只留最显眼的那条。这段补充之前会和「通常 1～3 条」叠在一起。离职这种一题里有年假、报销、电脑的问题，模型就只留下归还资产。多件事时不再附上那句普通上限。枚举题仍保留自己的上限说明，普通单题仍是通常 1 到 3 条。

作答提示也改过一句曾经帮倒忙的话。原先写：问题提到但原文没写的，单独说未检索到。发薪那题的正文已经写了银行假日提前发放，模型还是补了一句「未检索到银行放假怎么处理」。两句放在一起，就是自己打自己。

现在的要求是三条：

  1. 这件事原文已经回答了，按原文写完，不要再补未检索到。只有这件事在原文里完全没有着落，才单独写未检索到。
  2. 题目里已经给出的事实，拿去对照原文的条件。条件已经满足，就按原文的允许或禁止下结论。礼品那条禁止造成利益冲突。客户已经要求「优先考虑」，就写成不能接受，不要改成「如果没有冲突就可以收」。
  3. 不要先写一条原文没有的做法，再用未检索到把这条做法收回。离职里的「应结清年假」就是这种句子：原文没有折算，模型先写义务，再补一句没找到。

提示每调用读一次文件，不在进程里缓存。改 config/prompts.txt 之后，下一问就是新句子，不用为了提示重启。换模型仍要重启，因为模型名在进程启动时读。

核对是规则，不是再问一次模型

早期的核对只要「勾到了至少一条」就通过。权游的铁王座少写了宝剑，面板上仍是通过。星河上，礼品被答成可以收、离职被补上一句结清年假，也是通过。年假答成 7 天的那次，结论和依据对不上，核对同样放过。

现在多了三项，仍然不调用模型：

检查 拦住什么 放过什么
结论被收回 前面已经写出原文里的事实，后面又说未检索到同一件事 另一件事确实没有条文。金额题说「没有看到报销上限」可以留
义务没有依据 先写必须、应当、原则上，再用未检索到把这句收回 原文里本来就有的「原则上提前 30 日」
禁止被说成许可 原文是不能造成利益冲突，结论写成「如果没有就可以接受」 结论里仍然写着不能接受

空召回仍然失败。年终奖因此不会被说成有依据。句子按句号、问号、叹号和分号切开。模型用分号把「应结清」和「未检索到」粘在一句里时，早期切不开，核对会放过；补上分号之后，这句被拦住。

这三项也会误伤。Qwen3.6 把离职答对了：提前通知、报销、归还资产都在，年假写成「未检索到离职时怎么处理」，没有编结清。核对仍失败，因为「未检索到」那句和前面的通知都有「离职」两个字。拦住写反的结论，比放过它更值得。误伤要再收紧匹配，而不是退回「有条目就算过」。这一条还没改。

有上限的数量，让程序算

年假题是：已经结转 8 天，刚满一个工作年，最多还有多少天。原文是满一年 15 天，结转上限 30 天。8+15=23，没有顶到 30。

这条题在三个阶段的结论不一样：

阶段 结论 原因
手册还是章节树 7 天 漏了当时的结转上限那一节，核对仍通过
改成扁平问答，只靠提示 30 天 勾到了 15 天和 30 天上限，模型把上限当成他的余额
程序算出结果再写进结论 23 天 已有 8、新增 15、上限 30，取较小值

提示里已经写了「已有加新增，且不得超过上限，结论只写这一个数」。智谱仍写 30。于是不再指望它心算。

程序从问题里取「已经、已有、结转了」后面的数，从正文里取「享有、每满」后面的新增和「上限、最多、不超过」后面的上限。三种都恰好一个、单位都是天，才算 min(已有+新增, 上限)。这个数交给撰写和改写。答复的结论里如果没有这个数，就用算出来的句子换掉结论，依据段保留。已经写成 23 的草稿不会再被改一遍。

数字只来自问题和原文。问题里没有已有数量，或者正文里新增和上限对不上同一种单位，就不算，仍交给模型。8 加 15、上限若是 20，结果是 20，不会报出超过上限的和。

这道题因此稳定写成 23 天。Qwen3.6 上它耗时 12.3 秒，模型调用 4 次：勾选、撰写、以及数量放进上下文之后的改写。日志里能看到已有 8、新增 15、上限 30、结果 23。

改完之后，13 题变成什么样

同一套星河题，三次跑法叠在一起看，改动落在哪一目了然。

题 改提示前的智谱 改提示、数量和核对后的智谱 Qwen3.6
发薪，银行假日 写对了，又补未检索到 不再自相矛盾 通过
结转 8 天后再满一年 结论写成 30 天 程序改成 23 天 23 天
1800 礼品，要求优先考虑 改成可以接受 按禁止写 不能接受
绩效目标能否改 勾到举报那一条 仍勾 1.34，并编理由 勾回 1.19，仍缺评估周期
笔记本丢失 空召回 仍空 2 小时内上报
离职三件事 只留归还，并写结清 仍编结清，核对改为失败 通知、报销、归还都在，没有结清
年终奖 拒答 拒答 拒答

完全正确从 7 道到 10 道，再在 Qwen3.6 上到 11 道。智谱剩下的 3 道错，两道是勾选不听提示，一道是作答仍编义务。换模型补上了勾选，作答上的「必须」还在，所以离职是部分正确。

核对在 Qwen3.6 这轮是 11/13。年终奖空召回失败，这是预期。离职那道事实是对的，被「离职」两个字误伤，这是要再收的。

还没做、但已经想清楚的

模型不听提示的时候，程序仍能在它交卷之后动手，不必再加一轮对话：

  • 勾回来的编号，摘要和问题对不上，就丢掉。1.34 的摘要是举报，问题是绩效，这条不该留下。
  • 模型返回空数组时，问题里的「笔记本」和摘要里的「设备」若是上下位，本地可以留住这条，再送去作答。这和「向量当主检索」不是一件事。
  • 核对失败时，把那句没有依据的义务从给用户的文字里拿掉，而不是整段打回。

这三件都还没写进主路径。向量短名单也没有。35 到 100 条问答，标题和摘要一次放进上下文，在 256K 的窗口里很宽裕。慢和错都不来自「窗口装不下」。

慢来自小模型读完这份列表。错来自模型没有按摘要里的那句话勾，或者作答时补了原文没有的义务。换一个更听话的模型，笔记本和设备、离职的三件事，不用改检索架构也能对上。提示和核对仍然要在，因为换模型之前，这些错会直接出现在用户看到的句子里。

代码在 github.com/zealot2002/mycs：

做什么 哪里
提示，每次调用重读 config/prompts.txt
多件事不再叠普通条数上限 src/mycs/planning/flat_faq.py
已有数量加上限 src/mycs/skills/capped_quantity.py
规则核对 src/mycs/verifier.py
发布后才进入问答 frontend/src/views/KnowledgeDetailView.vue

上一篇是 三个模型，只改一个变量。系列从 RAG 的终点不是检索，而是知识 开始。

Frontend.title: 知识库定了，就别再让模型猜你在问什么
Frontend.summary:
上一篇说，Agent 该规划的是知识缺口，不是一串搜索词。

写代码的时候，这句话很快碰到一个更具体的事实：用户在界面上已经选好了知识库。这时再让模型判断「这是办件进度，还是政策问答」，多出来的那一次请求并不增加知识。

所以现在的主路径很短。

已选知识库
   ↓
把已上线问答的标题和摘要交给模型
   ↓
模型只返回编号
   ↓
按编号取出答案全文
   ↓
只根据这些全文写答复
   ↓
用规则核对，不让模型自己证明自己

下面这张图是同一次提问。左边是答复，右边是过程。第一步写着：知识库已选定，直接勾选问答，本步不调用大模型。第二次调用才出现，名字是 Qwen3.6，工作是看 FAQ 标题。整次耗时 5.6 秒。

问题是「工资一般什么时候发到账？如果碰到银行放假呢？」答复是：次月 5 个自然日内；碰到银行假日，提前到前一个工作日。这是库里那一条的原文，不是模型凭空补的。顶栏写着「星河科技员工手册（35 条）」。过程面板里，理解问题是编排，勾选才是大模型。

把这一步展开，能看见模型实际读到的东西和它交回来的东西。

输入是整份已上线标题。输出只有编号，这一次是 1.9。摘要写的是发薪和银行假日，和问题对得上。程序再按这个编号去取正文，后面才写答复。

这条路是从更长的链路里收出来的

第一篇里的知识世界有实体、关系、时间和证据。落地时我们先做成过一棵目录：章、节、叶子，计划阶段让模型点一个分支，再钻进去检索。星河手册的早期版本走的就是这条。

那一版上，同一类问题已经露出后来反复出现的三类错：

当时卡住的地方 实际发生过的事
计划 JSON 写坏 账号泄露那题，模型返回的计划不是合法 JSON，靠兜底计划才救回来
钻错章节 学习预算被钻进别的章，靠一次不限范围的重试才命中
漏掉同一章里的另一条 年假结转答成 7 天。当时的上限写在另一节，检索没把它带上，核对仍然通过

7 天这个数字后来没有沿用。手册改成现在这 35 条之后，条文本身也改过：满一年 15 天，结转上限 30 天。已有 8 天再满一年，是 23，不是 7，也不是把 30 直接当成余额。旧链路的教训留下来了：让模型决定「往哪一章钻」，它会钻偏，也会在钻对的时候漏掉旁边那一条。

扁平问答把「往哪钻」拿掉了。一份知识库就是一组并列的问和答。没有父子章节要先钻进去。界面上就是这张表。

知识库 已上线条数
流行音乐 30
三国演义 50
权游知识手册 50
潘多拉星球生态手册 50
宠物饲养指南 100
星河科技员工手册 35

叙事类的库，标题和问题几乎同形，勾选不难。星河是制度，问题经常换说法，一条问题里还叠着两三件事。后面两篇的测试，难的都在这本手册上。

模型只交编号

勾选时，模型看到的不是答案全文，而是每条的三样东西：

section_ref   编号，例如 1.9
title         问题
summary       答案开头

条数不超过 120 时，整份列表一次送进去。现在这六本都在这个限度里，所以都是一批。模型只许返回：

{"section_refs":["1.9"],"reason":""}

编号必须来自这次给它的列表。一条都对不上，就返回空数组。程序再丢掉不在列表里的编号。

空数组的含义是拒答，不是换个近题凑一条。年终奖怎么发，库里没有，就告诉用户没找到，不编一套发放规则。三国库里问铁王座、权游库里问罗贯中，走的也是这条：空召回，然后停。

勾中的编号才去数据库取答案全文，交给写答复的那一次调用。所以一次命中的问题，大模型通常只有两下：勾选，然后作答。年假这种要算数量的题会多一次改写，第四篇写它。一条都没勾上时，只有勾选那一次，后面的作答不再发生。

过程面板再往下是后半段：按编号读正文、规则核对、撰写回答。核对这一步标明不调用大模型。

同一套页面可以换库。下面这张图里，先问了发薪，再把顶栏换成三国演义，问关羽和刘备的关系、吕布的坐骑。后一问 8.9 秒，答复按库里的原句写了桃园之义和赤兔马。过程仍是「理解跳过，然后勾选」。

勾选上的几条硬规则

这些规则是程序的，不是模型临时发挥的。

规则 为什么这样定
120 条以内一次送完 分批会让模型在第一批就停。现在最大的一本是 100 条，还用不上分批
必须分批时，每一批都送 模型不能返回 done。停不停不是它的决定，程序把各批编号并起来
普通问题最后最多留 5 条 模型有时会勾一串沾边的标题。超出之后，用本地的词面重合把多出来的丢掉
枚举「有哪些、全部」最多留 24 条 金额限制这种题要的是一组，不是一条
多件事的题，不再附上「通常 1～3 条」 离职里同时有年假、报销、电脑。加上这句，模型只留下最显眼的归还资产
本地词面分只在超出上限时才用 它分不清「设备丢失」和「笔记本」。拿它当主检索，换一种说法就空

我们讨论过用向量相似度代替这次勾选。发布时把标题和摘要嵌进去，提问时做点积，50 到 100 条通常不到一秒，能躲开 7B 读完整份列表的那几十秒。它适合当短名单：先留大约 8 条，再让现在这次勾选在短名单里挑。若只用相似度当裁判，标题像的错条会留下。项目文档里的约定仍是提问时不做向量检索。短名单没有接进主路径。

踩坑

提示词还在说字典和父子。 早期召回沿着目录往下钻，提示词里有章、父节点、叶子。产品改成扁平问答之后，这些词还留在提示里，模型会去找一个不存在的层级。后来把勾选提示改成：你看到的就是并列条目，只勾摘要能直接回答的那些。

模型想自己决定「后面不用看了」。 列表太长、必须分批时，如果让模型返回 done，它可能在第一批就停，后面的正确条目再也看不到。程序的做法是：每一批都送，只收集编号，最后再并起来。

曾想把「理解问题」并进勾选，省一次请求。 省是省了，但勾选必须看见整份标题。把意图分类塞进同一次，提示更长，编号也更容易漂。知识库已经由人选定，理解这一步直接跳过就够了。没有选定知识库的办件、办事指南，仍走原来的理解。

标题像，不代表这条能回答。 提示写明：标题用词接近，但摘要里没有那件事，不要勾。同一件事的不同说法要勾，摘要用了上位词、下位词或同义说法，也算同一件事。笔记本和「设备丢失」就靠这句。这句写上之后，小模型仍会失手，那是它没有照着摘要里的那句话勾，放到第三篇的对照里。

测试题自己写错，会变成一条假缺陷。 「诸葛亮出征骑的什么马」在三国库里对不上。原题是坐骑，答案是四轮车，也叫素舆，不是马。模型勾到吕布的赤兔之后，正文写了未检索到，没有把赤兔安到诸葛亮头上。这题后来不计入。吕布的坐骑才是赤兔，上面那张切换知识库的图问的是这一条。

这一篇留下来的接口

写答复的模型只看见勾中的问答原文。数字、时限、对象、步骤都要从这些原文里来。没被勾中的事，不能靠模型的常识补上。

核对也不把「模型觉得自己对」当成通过。通过与否是程序拿答复和取回来的正文做的。它放过过什么、又拦住过什么，第四篇写。

代码在 github.com/zealot2002/mycs：

做什么 哪里
选定知识库就跳过理解 src/mycs/agent/loop.py
整表勾选、分批也走完 src/mycs/planning/flat_faq.py
勾选提示 config/prompts.txt 的 faq_title
超出条数才用的词面分 src/mycs/knowledge/search.py 的 score_entity
问答页和过程面板 frontend/src/views/ChatView.vue

下一篇看时间花在哪。同一条链路，换模型之后，慢的往往不是生成那几十个字。

Frontend.title: npm stopped taking weekends
Frontend.summary:
For six years, npm had the same week. Five busy days, then a Saturday and Sunday at about a quarter of the pace, because the people running npm install were at work and then they weren't.

Then in spring 2025 that started to go. npm's downloads API has a daily total for the whole registry going back to 2015, so here's a weekend day as a share of a weekday, quarter by quarter, with PyPI beside it:

A weekend day's downloads as a share of a weekday's, npm and PyPI (the data)

The median weekend day over the median weekday, each quarter. npm's from its downloads API, PyPI's
from ClickHouse's public ClickPy data. Days npm reports as zero
and the Christmas fortnight are left out, and 2026 Q4 runs to 19 November.

npm sat between 23% and 29% for 25 quarters in a row. It's at 47% now.

I was pulling those totals to see how big the AI boom looks from the registry's side, and the size is daft enough on its own. npm served 292 billion downloads in October 2024, 424 billion in October 2025 and just over a trillion this October.

But a bigger registry with the same weekly shape would just be more of the same. The extra downloads since summer 2024 run at 54% on weekends, so whatever's adding them barely keeps office hours. That's close to PyPI, which has been up there as far back as the data goes.

It isn't just the new stuff

The obvious answer is all the new apps AI tools are spinning up, installing whatever's in fashion. So I looked at packages nobody starts a project with any more.

node-sass has been deprecated on npm since 2024, with a notice telling you to use sass instead. In summer 2024 it got about 286,000 downloads on a normal weekday and 62,000 on a weekend day. Now it's 155,000 and 82,000. Fewer people install it on a Tuesday than two years ago, and more do on a Saturday. TSLint, which told everyone to move to ESLint back in 2019, has nearly doubled at weekends with its weekdays flat. And left-pad, of all things, went from 21% to 59%.

Weekend downloads as a share of weekday ones, then and now (the data)

Summer 2024 is July to September, autumn 2026 is 1 October to 19 November. Medians, like the chart
above.

Packages people still use moved just as much. When I checked 507 of the biggest on 14 November, 506 had gone up by at least 10 points, and none was still under 30%. Taking the biggest few hundred out of the registry's total leaves the line where it was, so it isn't a few giants dragging the average along.

vaul is my favourite. It's a drawer component for React, and its README opens with "This repo is unmaintained". The last release was December 2024. In summer 2024 it got 76,000 downloads a weekday, and now it gets 5.4 million, because the Radix version of shadcn/ui's drawer is built on it, and AI app builders like Lovable start you off with the whole shadcn set. Lovable also puts its own Vite plugin, lovable-tagger, in the projects it makes, and of the 76,416 package.json files on GitHub that list it, 75,904 list vaul too.

Linux went first

So who's installing node-sass on a Saturday? A download count doesn't say who asked for it, but packages with a separate binary for each platform give a hint. esbuild ships one for Linux, one for Macs, one for Windows and a pile of others, and npm only fetches the one for the machine it's running on.

Linux stopped taking weekends before Macs and Windows did (the data)

Weekend downloads as a share of weekday ones for @esbuild/linux-x64, @esbuild/darwin-arm64 and
@esbuild/win32-x64, worked out the same way as the first chart.

Linux started drifting in spring 2025, while the Mac and Windows binaries didn't budge all year. They only got going in 2026, and they're at 44% and 45% now to Linux's 54%. Rollup's binaries do exactly the same. Linux is also where the volume is: 59 million esbuild installs a weekday, up from 5 million in summer 2024, against 3.5 million for Macs.

That gap rules out one boring answer. Anything that grabs packages wholesale, like a mirror or a security scanner, would fetch all three alike, and the three lines would have moved together. They didn't.

Most CI runners, containers and cloud sandboxes are Linux, so the first wave looks like machines. OpenAI's Codex cloud agent and Claude Code's general release both came out in May 2025, which lines up nicely and proves nothing. I can't read the Macs and Windows PCs. That could be people building things at weekends now that something else does the typing, or more CI on Macs, or both, and download counts can't tell them apart.

The weirdest one I found is create-vite, the thing you run to start a new Vite project. Scaffolders were always weekend-heavy, because starting a side project is a Saturday thing, and create-vite ran at 67% in summer 2024. It's at 93% now, on 12 times the volume. Vite projects get started on a Sunday nearly as often as on a Tuesday.

Checking a package yourself

This gets a package's last month from the same API and gives you its weekend average as a percentage of its weekday one:

curl -s https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/range/last-month/react | jq '
  [.downloads[] | select(.downloads > 0) | {
    n: .downloads,
    weekend: (.day | strptime("%Y-%m-%d") | mktime | strftime("%a") | test("Sat|Sun"))
  }]
  | group_by(.weekend) | map(map(.n) | add / length)
  | .[1] / .[0] * 100 | round'

It's a straight average over the last 30 days rather than the medians in the charts, so it won't match them exactly. react comes out at 57 today, and node-sass at 46. In the summer of 2024, almost everything came out somewhere around 25.

vaul's README still says it's unmaintained. Last Sunday it was downloaded 3.3 million times.

DevOps.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
DevOps.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

DevOps.title: Indexing 206M+ Podcast Subtitle Lines and Pairing Them with PubMed & Wikipedia Citations
DevOps.summary:
When I research a topic through long-form podcasts or university lectures (say, sleep architecture, creatine for cognition, or semiconductor supply chains), I keep hitting two annoying walls:

  1. Searching YouTube drops you into three-hour episodes full of sponsor reads and detours.
  2. Dropping a link into an LLM summarizer strips away the speaker's actual tone, caveats, and source provenance.

Over the past few weeks I built PastNoise to scratch that exact itch. Instead of generating another text summary, it searches across 206M+ timestamped spoken subtitle lines and stitches 5 to 6 non-duplicate primary speakers into a single continuous screening room, paired with side-by-side Wikipedia, PubMed, Crossref, and OpenAlex citations.

Three Small Engineering Choices That Made the Biggest Difference

1. Filtering sponsor reads before picking clips (not after)
Early builds looked fine until a flagship topic pulled two Hostinger and Tonal ad reads from top podcasts. Moving a strict sponsor/outro detector ahead of act selection and hydrating 16 candidate windows first (then backfilling clean distinct channels) dropped sponsor contamination to zero across all 58 indexed screenings.

2. Rendering full bilingual transcripts in SSR DOM with #act-X-t-Y citation anchors
Single-page tabs that unmount transcript DOM hide 95% of spoken text from search engines and make it impossible to quote a speaker accurately. Keeping every chapter's timestamped transcript inside lightweight

accordions with click-to-copy citation links lets readers jump straight to the exact second and verify the primary quote.

3. Preserving original subtitle sequence IDs (origSeq) when splitting long cues
Auto-captions often pack 220+ characters into one cue. Splitting cues down to readable 96-character lines broke pre-translated subtitle lookups whenever the original sequence index passed 100. Keeping an explicit origSeq field alongside sequential display IDs solved alignment cleanly for English, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese (via OpenCC at zero extra LLM cost).

Open Assets You Can Reuse (CC BY 4.0)

If you prefer local notes or want clean benchmark data for citation-grounded RAG experiments, I exported the entire 58-topic curated archive under CC BY 4.0:

  • Obsidian Knowledge Vault (58 dossiers + 25 Thinker MOCs): github.com/nonacosa/pastnoise-obsidian-vault
  • Hugging Face Dataset (491 ad-filtered clips with YouTube timestamps + DOIs): huggingface.co/datasets/pkwenda/pastnoise-primary-citations
  • Free Hydration Utility: Galpin Equation Hydration Calculator
  • Full Interactive Screening Room (free without login): pastnoise.com

Curious how other builders here handle long-form audio/video retrieval and hallucination checks without losing the original speaker's voice.

DevOps.title: I Built a Visual Subnet Planning Tool for Cloud & DevOps Engineers

Planning IP ranges and subnet allocations across cloud environments can quickly become messy.

Whether you're working with AWS VPCs, Azure VNets, GCP VPC networks, Kubernetes clusters, or on-premises infrastructure, CIDR planning is something we deal with regularly.

I built Subnets Preview to make this process more visual and easier to manage.

  • Split & Join CIDR blocks — divide address ranges and visualize subnet allocations.
  • Name & Color Subnets — organize networks by purpose, environment, or workload.
  • Export PNG — turn your subnet layout into a visual network reference.
  • Import & Export JSON — save, reuse, and version-control your designs.
  • Share via URL — collaborate by sharing subnet layouts.
  • VS Code / Cursor Extension — preview local subnet designs directly in your editor.

Where is it useful?

  • Planning Virtual Network address spaces.
  • Avoiding overlapping IP ranges across environments.
  • Documenting and visualizing network layouts before implementing them with Terraform or other IaC tools.

DevOps.title: Stop Deploying Manually: I Built a CI/CD Pipeline on AWS ECS Fargategs
DevOps.summary:
By Muhammad Bilal Sharif Bukhari · GitHub → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → ECR → ECS Fargate

The 3 a.m. problem every developer knows

My client Lucy had a simple Dockerized 2048 game and a painful release routine: build the image on a laptop, push it by hand, open the AWS console, update the service, refresh the page, and pray.

One typo in a tag, one forgotten step, and the site was down. Every update took longer than the change itself.

So I gave myself one rule for this project: git push is the only deployment step. Everything after it must happen on its own.

Here is how I built it, and every wall I hit on the way.

What I built

A fully automated CI/CD pipeline on AWS (region us-east-1):

  1. A push to GitHub triggers AWS CodePipeline.
  2. AWS CodeBuild pulls the code, builds the Docker image, and tags it.
  3. The image is pushed to Amazon ECR.
  4. Amazon ECS on Fargate starts a new task with the fresh image and removes the old one.

No servers to patch. No manual builds. No console clicking.

The toolkit

Service Its job
GitHub Source of truth and the pipeline trigger
AWS CodePipeline Orchestrates Source → Build → Deploy
AWS CodeBuild Builds and tags the Docker image
Amazon ECR Private registry that stores the images
Amazon ECS (Fargate) Runs the container with no servers to manage
IAM roles and policies Let each service securely talk to the others

Step 1: ECR repository and ECS cluster

I started with the foundations: a private ECR repository (game-2048-repo) and an ECS cluster (game-2048-cluster) using the Fargate launch type. For the task definition I chose a larger task size than the minimum, because I wanted the game to stay smooth and I didn't want resource limits to be a variable while debugging.

Before going further, I checked everything from the CLI. This habit saved me hours later, because the console can look fine while the wiring underneath is wrong.

aws ecs list-clusters
aws ecs list-services --cluster game-2048-cluster

Step 2: Containerizing the game

The game is static files served by Nginx, so the Dockerfile stays tiny:

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY . /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80

I pushed the project to GitHub with a first commit. That repository became the trigger for everything else.

Step 3: CodeBuild, the engine room

CodeBuild reads a buildspec.yml from the repo. Mine logs in to ECR, builds, tags, pushes, and writes a small file called imagedefinitions.json that tells ECS which image to run.

version: 0.2
phases:
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $ECR_URI
  build:
    commands:
      - docker build -t game-2048-repo .
      - docker tag game-2048-repo:latest $ECR_URI/game-2048-repo:latest
  post_build:
    commands:
      - docker push $ECR_URI/game-2048-repo:latest
      - printf '[{"name":"2048-container","imageUri":"%s"}]' $ECR_URI/game-2048-repo:latest > imagedefinitions.json
artifacts:
  files: imagedefinitions.json

Step 4: CodePipeline, connecting the dots

The last step was wiring three stages together: Source (GitHub), Build (CodeBuild), Deploy (ECS). When all three turned green, I pushed a tiny change and watched the whole thing roll out without touching the console.

🚧 Everything that broke (so yours doesn't)

This is the part I wish I'd read before starting. Every item below cost me real time.

1. CodeBuild couldn't push to ECR: no basic auth credentials

My first build died within seconds of reaching the push step. I double-checked the repo name, the region, and the login command, and all of them were right. The real culprit was the CodeBuild service role, which had no ECR permissions at all.

Fix: attach AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPowerUser (or a tighter custom policy) to the role.

Lesson: when AWS says "auth," check the IAM role before you check your code.

2. Cannot connect to the Docker daemon

The build started, then failed the moment it ran docker build. CodeBuild doesn't allow Docker-in-Docker by default.

Fix: enable Privileged mode in the CodeBuild environment settings. It's one checkbox, and it's easy to miss.

3. Docker Hub toomanyrequests

One run worked and the next failed with a rate-limit error while pulling the base image. Shared build infrastructure hits Docker Hub's anonymous limits fast.

Fix: pull the base image from the Amazon ECR Public Gallery, or authenticate to Docker Hub inside the build.

4. The Deploy stage failed with an invalid imagedefinitions.json

This one humbled me. Source and Build were green, but Deploy kept failing, and I spent far too long staring at the pipeline instead of at the file. The name inside imagedefinitions.json must match the container name in the ECS task definition exactly, character for character. Mine had a small mismatch.

Fix: copy the container name from the task definition instead of typing it from memory, and make sure the file is declared under artifacts in buildspec.yml.

5. The task started and stopped immediately

The service kept launching tasks that died in seconds. The console said very little until I opened the stopped task and read the stopped reason, then checked the CloudWatch logs.

Fix: correct the container port to match the Dockerfile (80) and make sure the task has an execution role.

6. Task "Running," but the website wouldn't load

The most frustrating one, because everything looked healthy. The task was running and the pipeline was green, yet the browser just spun.

Fix: the security group. I needed to allow inbound HTTP on port 80, and the task needed a public IP to be reachable.

7. The browser shows "Not secure"

I hit this once the site finally loaded. It isn't a bug. It's plain HTTP.

Fix for production: put an Application Load Balancer with an ACM certificate in front of the service.

8. The ECS service never reached a steady state

Tasks kept being created, failing, and being replaced. ECS simply couldn't pull the image.

Fix: make sure the task execution role has AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy, and that the subnet has a network path to ECR (public IP, NAT gateway, or VPC endpoints).

9. The pipeline was green, but I still saw the old game

I pushed a visible change and the page didn't change. The pipeline was fine. The browser was caching, and I was reusing the latest tag.

Fix: hard-refresh first. For anything beyond a lab, tag images with the commit SHA so every release is traceable and rollbacks are easy.

10. Leftover resources

A pipeline, a cluster, a service, and a registry full of images don't clean themselves up.

Fix: when the project is finished, delete the service, cluster, pipeline, CodeBuild project, and ECR images.

💡 What I learned

  • IAM is where most failures live. Nearly every error was some version of "service A isn't allowed to do X to service B." Learning to read those errors was the biggest skill I gained.
  • Exact names matter. One mismatched container name broke an entire deployment.
  • Logs beat guessing. CodeBuild logs and CloudWatch told me what was wrong every single time. I just had to read them first.
  • Fargate removes servers, not networking. Security groups, subnets, and public IPs still decide whether your app is reachable.
  • Verify from the CLI. The console shows what you think you built. The CLI shows what actually exists.
  • latest is a lab tag, not a production strategy. Version your images.
  • Working for a real client changes how you build. I had to explain why each service existed, not just make it work.

What I'd add next

  • A test stage (linting or unit tests) before deployment
  • An Application Load Balancer + HTTPS
  • Infrastructure as Code with Terraform or CloudFormation
  • Blue/green deployments for zero-downtime releases
  • CloudWatch alarms for task health

Final thoughts

I started with a game and finished with a real DevOps workflow: GitHub → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → ECR → ECS Fargate, fully automated and serverless.

The best part is the feeling. I changed a line of code, pushed it, made a cup of tea, and the live site had already updated.

Thank you to Lucy for trusting me with this project. 🙌

If you're learning AWS, build this one. Nothing teaches you how CI/CD really works like watching it fail, fixing it, and seeing it go green.

What was the first thing that broke in your first pipeline? Tell me in the comments. 👇

Connect with me on LinkedIn and GitHub.

1. The Dual-Engine Architecture Explained

Most developers make a critical mistake when setting up local AI coding: they try to use a single large model (like a 14B or 32B model) for both chat reasoning and inline tab autocompletion.

Inline tab completion requires instantaneous latency—under 50 milliseconds. If you have to pause for 600ms while typing a function header, your flow state is broken. Conversely, chat and whole-file refactoring require deep reasoning and broad context.

The optimal architecture splits the workload across two specialized local models:

Engine A: Inline Autocomplete qwen2.5-coder:1.5b-base 22ms – 38ms Instant single-line & multi-line code prediction on Tab key.
Engine B: Chat & Refactoring qwen2.5-coder:7b-instruct (or 14B / 32B) 250ms – 600ms (TTFT) Architecture design, unit test writing, bug analysis, refactoring.

# 2. Pull the high-accuracy chat & refactoring model
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b

Important: Always ensure you pull 1.5b-base rather than 1.5b-instruct for autocomplete. Base models excel at raw text/code continuation without injecting unwanted conversational headers.

Tuning the Chat Modelfile for Code Generation

# System prompt enforcing production-grade engineering output

Build the customized model:

ollama create qwen-coder-dev -f ./qwen-coder-dev.modelfile

To integrate local models seamlessly into your editor with identical keybindings and UI to GitHub Copilot and Cursor, install the open-source Continue extension:

Open your Continue configuration file (located at ~/.continue/config.json or by clicking the gear icon in the Continue sidebar). Replace its contents with this optimized configuration:

If you experience stutter during completions, ensure OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1 is set in your environment variables. Flash Attention compresses the KV-cache representation by 45%, allowing the model to stay entirely inside memory.

Backend.title: npm stopped taking weekends
Backend.summary:
For six years, npm had the same week. Five busy days, then a Saturday and Sunday at about a quarter of the pace, because the people running npm install were at work and then they weren't.

Then in spring 2025 that started to go. npm's downloads API has a daily total for the whole registry going back to 2015, so here's a weekend day as a share of a weekday, quarter by quarter, with PyPI beside it:

A weekend day's downloads as a share of a weekday's, npm and PyPI (the data)

The median weekend day over the median weekday, each quarter. npm's from its downloads API, PyPI's
from ClickHouse's public ClickPy data. Days npm reports as zero
and the Christmas fortnight are left out, and 2026 Q4 runs to 19 November.

npm sat between 23% and 29% for 25 quarters in a row. It's at 47% now.

I was pulling those totals to see how big the AI boom looks from the registry's side, and the size is daft enough on its own. npm served 292 billion downloads in October 2024, 424 billion in October 2025 and just over a trillion this October.

But a bigger registry with the same weekly shape would just be more of the same. The extra downloads since summer 2024 run at 54% on weekends, so whatever's adding them barely keeps office hours. That's close to PyPI, which has been up there as far back as the data goes.

It isn't just the new stuff

The obvious answer is all the new apps AI tools are spinning up, installing whatever's in fashion. So I looked at packages nobody starts a project with any more.

node-sass has been deprecated on npm since 2024, with a notice telling you to use sass instead. In summer 2024 it got about 286,000 downloads on a normal weekday and 62,000 on a weekend day. Now it's 155,000 and 82,000. Fewer people install it on a Tuesday than two years ago, and more do on a Saturday. TSLint, which told everyone to move to ESLint back in 2019, has nearly doubled at weekends with its weekdays flat. And left-pad, of all things, went from 21% to 59%.

Weekend downloads as a share of weekday ones, then and now (the data)

Summer 2024 is July to September, autumn 2026 is 1 October to 19 November. Medians, like the chart
above.

Packages people still use moved just as much. When I checked 507 of the biggest on 14 November, 506 had gone up by at least 10 points, and none was still under 30%. Taking the biggest few hundred out of the registry's total leaves the line where it was, so it isn't a few giants dragging the average along.

vaul is my favourite. It's a drawer component for React, and its README opens with "This repo is unmaintained". The last release was December 2024. In summer 2024 it got 76,000 downloads a weekday, and now it gets 5.4 million, because the Radix version of shadcn/ui's drawer is built on it, and AI app builders like Lovable start you off with the whole shadcn set. Lovable also puts its own Vite plugin, lovable-tagger, in the projects it makes, and of the 76,416 package.json files on GitHub that list it, 75,904 list vaul too.

Linux went first

So who's installing node-sass on a Saturday? A download count doesn't say who asked for it, but packages with a separate binary for each platform give a hint. esbuild ships one for Linux, one for Macs, one for Windows and a pile of others, and npm only fetches the one for the machine it's running on.

Linux stopped taking weekends before Macs and Windows did (the data)

Weekend downloads as a share of weekday ones for @esbuild/linux-x64, @esbuild/darwin-arm64 and
@esbuild/win32-x64, worked out the same way as the first chart.

Linux started drifting in spring 2025, while the Mac and Windows binaries didn't budge all year. They only got going in 2026, and they're at 44% and 45% now to Linux's 54%. Rollup's binaries do exactly the same. Linux is also where the volume is: 59 million esbuild installs a weekday, up from 5 million in summer 2024, against 3.5 million for Macs.

That gap rules out one boring answer. Anything that grabs packages wholesale, like a mirror or a security scanner, would fetch all three alike, and the three lines would have moved together. They didn't.

Most CI runners, containers and cloud sandboxes are Linux, so the first wave looks like machines. OpenAI's Codex cloud agent and Claude Code's general release both came out in May 2025, which lines up nicely and proves nothing. I can't read the Macs and Windows PCs. That could be people building things at weekends now that something else does the typing, or more CI on Macs, or both, and download counts can't tell them apart.

The weirdest one I found is create-vite, the thing you run to start a new Vite project. Scaffolders were always weekend-heavy, because starting a side project is a Saturday thing, and create-vite ran at 67% in summer 2024. It's at 93% now, on 12 times the volume. Vite projects get started on a Sunday nearly as often as on a Tuesday.

Checking a package yourself

This gets a package's last month from the same API and gives you its weekend average as a percentage of its weekday one:

curl -s https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/range/last-month/react | jq '
  [.downloads[] | select(.downloads > 0) | {
    n: .downloads,
    weekend: (.day | strptime("%Y-%m-%d") | mktime | strftime("%a") | test("Sat|Sun"))
  }]
  | group_by(.weekend) | map(map(.n) | add / length)
  | .[1] / .[0] * 100 | round'

It's a straight average over the last 30 days rather than the medians in the charts, so it won't match them exactly. react comes out at 57 today, and node-sass at 46. In the summer of 2024, almost everything came out somewhere around 25.

vaul's README still says it's unmaintained. Last Sunday it was downloaded 3.3 million times.

Backend.title: HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout (nginx): causes & fix
Backend.summary:
nginx reached the backend but did not get a response within the configured timeout (60 seconds by default).

Common causes

  • Long-running requests: large uploads, exports, reports, image processing.
  • The PHP-FPM pool is full (pm.max_children reached) and new requests wait in line.
  • Slow or locked database queries.
  • fastcgi_read_timeout or proxy_read_timeout too low for the use case.
  • Backend on another host unreachable through network or firewall (connect runs into the timeout).

How to check it

Find timeouts in the nginx log

grep 'upstream timed out' /var/log/nginx/error.log | tail -n 20

Check whether PHP-FPM hits its limit

grep -i 'max_children' /var/log/php8.3-fpm.log

Measure response time precisely

curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'connect=%{time_connect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n' https://cloud.example.com/status.php

What actually helps

  1. Fix the cause first: optimise slow queries, add indexes, move long jobs to cron or a queue.
  2. Raise pm.max_children according to RAM (RAM for PHP divided by memory per worker).
  3. Raise timeouts together: fastcgi_read_timeout 300s; in nginx plus max_execution_time and request_terminate_timeout in PHP-FPM.

FAQ

Should I just set the timeout to 3600 seconds?

No. It hides the problem and ties up workers. Raise timeouts only for specific locations such as upload or export paths.

Why do I get a 504 while PHP keeps running?

nginx only drops the connection to the client. The PHP script continues until max_execution_time or request_terminate_timeout kicks in.

Full page with every command and the German/Italian version: daniele-michelin.com/en/errors/http-504-gateway-timeout/

First published at daniele-michelin.com. The error lexicon covers HTTP, DNS, TLS, mail, database, PHP, nginx, systemd and Nextcloud, in German, English and Italian.

Backend.title: UG35 payload logs in Python — make timestamp pairing respect clock uncertainty
Backend.summary:
An image file and an event log each contain a timestamp. A developer sorts both exports, finds the closest event for every image and stores the pair. The resulting table looks complete even when the two clocks differ by several milliseconds. The algorithm also returns a pair when two events are equally plausible. A small timestamp residual can therefore hide a large uncertainty about which event belongs to an image.

This tutorial builds an offline pairing check for a payload integration project. The UNITED UAV UG35 mission-payload VTOL supplies the aircraft context. UNITED UAV publishes this tutorial and the linked listing. The program uses synthetic records and a timing contract supplied to the program. A team would need to establish that contract for the actual recorder, instrument and payload configuration before processing field exports.

The useful output is a decision with its evidence. Some frames have a unique candidate that stays inside the tolerance for every error allowed by the model. Other frames have a possible candidate whose interval crosses the acceptance boundary. A third group has several possible events. Keeping these outcomes visible lets the next stage request more evidence instead of silently accepting whichever row happened to sort first.

Define what each recorded time represents

Write down the event that opens the timestamp. An image record might identify the beginning of exposure, the end of exposure, the instant a trigger arrives or the time a file is written. A separate instrument might report acquisition time or publication time. Comparing those values requires knowing how the represented events relate. A clock correction cannot remove an unexplained delay between physical acquisition and a later software event.

For the example, assume the integration team has already converted both streams into integer nanoseconds against declared time origins. The timestamps may be relative to an epoch or a run start. They must use the same unit and have a defined mapping between clock domains. The code receives an offset that converts a frame timestamp into the event clock. Adding a positive offset moves the frame later on that clock. State this sign convention in the import contract and test it with a known pair.

Keep raw timestamp text and units in the archived export. Normalization should produce a new field while preserving the source value. A monotonic counter that resets at power-up needs a boot or run identity. Reusing the same counter range after a reset can make an old event appear to be a current candidate. Partition the imports by the identities that define a continuous clock domain before constructing the index.

Separate offset, error bound and tolerance

The offset is the estimated clock correction. The error bound describes how far the corrected timing difference could depart from its estimate under the stated model. The tolerance is the application's maximum accepted separation between represented events. These quantities serve different purposes. Increasing the tolerance to make a problematic export produce more matches changes the acceptance criterion.

Suppose the frame timestamp contributes a bounded error of one millisecond, the event timestamp contributes half a millisecond, and the clock correction contributes one and a half milliseconds. A conservative bound on their combined difference is three milliseconds. Summing the absolute bounds requires no assumption of statistical independence. Each component must itself be a justified bound over the interval being processed.

A standard deviation or a typical synchronization error needs a stated statistical model before it can support a different kind of decision. The code below expects a deterministic bound with coverage defined by the integration team. Its classifications remain conditional on that bound. A calibration observed once at the beginning of a recording also needs a model for how far clocks may drift afterward.

Derive possible and certain candidates

Let the corrected frame time be the frame timestamp plus the offset. Subtract an event timestamp to obtain the estimated difference. If the total error bound is R, the allowed difference lies between that estimate minus R and that estimate plus R. For a tolerance T, the accepted difference interval runs from negative T through positive T, including both endpoints.

An event is possible when its allowed difference interval intersects the accepted interval. Algebraically, the absolute estimated difference must be at most T plus R. This is the interval used to search for candidates. An event is certainly inside the timing tolerance under this bounded model when the absolute estimated difference plus R is at most T. That second condition asks whether the whole allowed interval lies inside the acceptance interval.

These conditions leave a useful middle region. An estimated difference of eight milliseconds, an error bound of three milliseconds and a tolerance of ten milliseconds produce an allowed difference from five through eleven milliseconds. The intervals overlap, so the event is possible. Part of the allowed difference exceeds ten, so the timing evidence is insufficient to classify the whole interval as acceptable.

Keep every possible event in the candidate set

Consider a corrected frame at one hundred milliseconds and events at one hundred and one hundred thirteen milliseconds. With a tolerance of ten and an error bound of three, both events are possible. The nearer event is entirely inside the tolerance. The second event touches the permitted boundary under one allowed timing error. A program that checks the nearest row alone hides that second candidate.

Returning several candidates is an honest outcome when the evidence permits several associations. An event sequence identifier, a hardware trigger count or another independently established relationship might resolve the association later. Record the rule and evidence used for that resolution. Choosing the smallest file name or the first row in an export would introduce a tie-breaking policy with no physical basis.

For this tutorial, a single possible event whose entire interval is acceptable receives a unique-within-bound status. A single possible event whose interval crosses the threshold receives an uncertain-time status. Multiple possible events receive an ambiguous status. No possible event receives a no-candidate status. These describe the relationship between the supplied records and timing model. They do not establish completeness of the event export.

Search an immutable sorted index

Construct the event index once for a batch of frames. Validate that event identifiers are unique and that times are sorted in nondecreasing order. Two different events can legitimately have equal timestamps when the recorder's resolution is coarse. Preserve both rows so the pairing decision can expose the ambiguity. Repeated event identifiers need reconciliation before indexing because two different rows cannot both stand for one stable identity.

For each frame, binary search locates the first event at or above the lower possible boundary and the first event strictly above the upper possible boundary. The second search includes an event exactly at the upper endpoint. Replacing it with a left-boundary search would lose that boundary case. Python's bisection functions define these insertion-point conventions. Python bisect documentation

The index copies the supplied events and timestamp keys into tuples. Each frozen event object preserves the values used during lookup. This avoids a caller changing the original list while frames are processed. After linear initialization, a lookup costs logarithmic search plus work proportional to the returned candidate count. If a very wide bound admits most of the batch, the large candidate set reflects the model's limited discrimination.

Implement the bounded join

The following Python 3.11 example uses integer timestamps throughout the comparisons. It rejects floats and booleans for time and bound fields. This catches accidental unit or parser conversions before they influence the decision. Integer nanoseconds are a convenient representation here, while the actual measurement resolution belongs in the import metadata.

The calibration validity interval is expressed in the original frame clock, including both endpoints. A frame outside that interval raises a validation error. Both the offset estimate and the combined bound must remain applicable throughout the interval. A calibration that needs several segments can produce a separate index configuration for each segment with the same event data and its own coverage. Handle the boundaries of those segments explicitly.

from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Event:
    event_id: str
    time_ns: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Match:
    event_id: str
    earliest_delta_ns: int
    latest_delta_ns: int
    certain_within_tolerance: bool


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Pairing:
    status: str
    candidates: tuple[Match, ...]


def integer(value: int, name: str) -> int:
    if type(value) is not int:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} must be an integer")
    return value


class TimeJoin:
    def __init__(
        self,
        events: list[Event],
        offset_ns: int,
        error_bound_ns: int,
        tolerance_ns: int,
        valid_from_frame_ns: int,
        valid_to_frame_ns: int,
    ):
        self.offset = integer(offset_ns, "offset_ns")
        self.bound = integer(error_bound_ns, "error_bound_ns")
        self.tolerance = integer(tolerance_ns, "tolerance_ns")
        self.valid_from = integer(valid_from_frame_ns, "valid_from_frame_ns")
        self.valid_to = integer(valid_to_frame_ns, "valid_to_frame_ns")
        if self.bound < 0 or self.tolerance < 0 or self.valid_from > self.valid_to:
            raise ValueError("negative bound/tolerance or reversed validity interval")

        self.events = tuple(events)
        self.times = tuple(integer(event.time_ns, "event.time_ns") for event in self.events)
        identifiers = [event.event_id for event in self.events]
        if any(not name or name.strip() != name for name in identifiers):
            raise ValueError("event identifiers must be nonempty and trimmed")
        if len(set(identifiers)) != len(identifiers):
            raise ValueError("duplicate event identifiers")
        if any(left > right for left, right in zip(self.times, self.times[1:])):
            raise ValueError("event times must be sorted")

    def pair(self, frame_ns: int) -> Pairing:
        frame_ns = integer(frame_ns, "frame_ns")
        if not self.valid_from <= frame_ns <= self.valid_to:
            raise ValueError("frame falls outside calibration validity")
        target = frame_ns + self.offset
        radius = self.tolerance + self.bound
        lo = bisect_left(self.times, target - radius)
        hi = bisect_right(self.times, target + radius)
        matches = []
        for event in self.events[lo:hi]:
            delta = target - event.time_ns
            matches.append(Match(
                event.event_id,
                delta - self.bound,
                delta + self.bound,
                abs(delta) + self.bound <= self.tolerance,
            ))
        if not matches:
            return Pairing("no_candidate", ())
        if len(matches) > 1:
            return Pairing("ambiguous", tuple(matches))
        status = "unique_within_bound" if matches[0].certain_within_tolerance else "uncertain_time"
        return Pairing(status, tuple(matches))

Exercise the decision boundaries

Use synthetic event times of one hundred and two hundred milliseconds, a zero offset, a three millisecond bound and a ten millisecond tolerance. A frame at one hundred six milliseconds has a single possible event at one hundred. Its difference interval is three through nine milliseconds, so it is unique within the bound. Moving the frame to one hundred eight makes the difference interval five through eleven, producing uncertain time.

A frame at one hundred fourteen milliseconds has no possible event in this example. Its nearest event differs by fourteen milliseconds and the sum of tolerance and bound is thirteen. The exact thirteen millisecond boundary still supplies a possible match because the intervals touch. Add another event at one hundred thirteen and process a frame at one hundred. The result becomes ambiguous even though the event at one hundred has an estimated difference of zero.

Test offset direction with a frame at ninety milliseconds, an event at one hundred and a positive ten millisecond correction. Then reverse the sign in a separate case and check the changed result. Include zero tolerance with a zero bound, negative timestamps for a relative origin and a bound larger than tolerance. When R exceeds T, no candidate can have its entire interval inside tolerance, even when its estimated difference is zero.

Validate the assumptions around the function

The class cannot infer the clock domain from an integer. The calling importer should bind the event clock identifier, frame clock identifier, calibration revision, time unit and run identity before constructing the index. Store those fields with the batch result. A timing outcome without the version of its correction and bound cannot be reproduced after calibration data changes.

Check the span of the event export as well. If the file ends early, a unique candidate near the end may be the only surviving record from several events that actually occurred. An importer can record the expected acquisition period, file sequence checks and any observed gaps separately. The pairer's output should preserve these coverage limitations so a downstream user can determine whether the batch meets its own acceptance requirements.

An offset that varies over a recording needs either a time-dependent correction or bounded segments. As an illustrative calculation, a relative rate bound of twenty parts per million accumulates as much as six milliseconds over three hundred seconds. Add that drift allowance to the applicable error model, or shorten the calibration coverage. This arithmetic describes the synthetic assumption. It supplies no clock-accuracy figure for the aircraft or a proposed payload.

Distinguish local pairing from batch assignment

The function considers each frame independently. Two frames may both return the same unique event. That can be valid if the event marks a state relevant to several images. If the application expects every trigger to produce exactly one frame, the batch has an additional cardinality constraint. Build the frame-to-event candidate relationships first and then evaluate whether a one-to-one assignment exists and whether it is unique.

Greedily assigning the nearest event to the earliest frame can consume a candidate required by a later frame. A batch assignment solver needs its own explicit policy for missing frames, extra events and temporal ordering. Keep that decision separate from the interval calculation so the evidence for possible correspondence remains inspectable. An assignment chosen to minimize total residual can still have alternatives with similar residuals.

Reprocessing should retain the original pairing report. A changed offset, drift allowance or tolerance can alter both candidate membership and status. Compare results by stable frame and event identities and explain why a previous association changed. If the batch supports inspection annotations, keep those annotations bound to the underlying image identity while flagging any changed event association for review.

Ask for a timing contract with the payload configuration

Before implementing a production importer, request representative unmodified image and event exports from the exact proposed payload configuration. Ask which physical event each timestamp represents, what survives a restart and which clock supplies the time. Request the evidence used to establish the correction, its sign, its coverage interval and the error bound under the operating conditions the integration will encounter.

Use the UG35 product reference to identify the aircraft platform during that discussion, then bind the timing contract to the actual recorder and instrument revisions. A product name alone supplies no export schema or synchronization method. Once the agreed fields are available, test deliberate clock shifts and duplicate timestamp cases alongside a normal batch. The resulting report can show which pairs remain supported, which require another identifier and which records have no admissible counterpart.

This article and its code were developed with AI assistance. The executable examples use synthetic data, with boundary cases checked locally before publication.

Backend.title: AI-Based Plant Stress Detection & Early Health Monitor (BAI507P): Complete Backend, Frontend, ML & Windows Setup Guide
Backend.summary:
This guide walks through every single file, function, ML decision, and setup step behind our AI-Based Plant Stress Detection and Early Health Monitoring System (BAI507P Mini Project). It is written so you can open the code in VS Code, trace every line from the browser to Python and SQLite, run it on Windows, and answer any viva question confidently.

1. End-to-End Architecture: How Everything Connects 

Browser (static/index.html)
  │  1. Captures / uploads a leaf photo + soil/weather slider values
  │  2. Sends multipart FormData via fetch("POST /api/analyze")
  ▼
FastAPI Server (app.py)
  │  3. Reads uploaded image bytes + validates sensor inputs
  │  4. Calls analyze_plant_image() in engine.py
  ▼
OpenCV Computer Vision Pipeline (engine.py)
  │  5. Segments plant tissue (HSV) & auto-centers the leaf (_center_plant_frame)
  │  6. Quantifies 6 visual symptoms:
  │     - Healthy Green %, Yellowing %, Browning %, Dark Spots %, Pale %, Wilting Index
  │  7. Draws color-coded segmentation overlay & encodes JPEG as base64
  ▼
Scikit-learn Multi-Modal Fusion (engine.py)
  │  8. Compares sensor values against the selected species' ideal range (deltas)
  │  9. Combines 6 visual features + 5 environmental features = 11 features
  │ 10. RandomForestClassifier predicts stress class + probabilities
  │ 11. Computes 0–100 Severity Score, Risk Level, Trend (Improving/Stable/Worsening) & Care Plan
  ▼
SQLite Database (db.py → plant_monitor.db)
  │ 12. Saves observation for historical progression charts & CSV export
  ▼
Browser (static/index.html)
     13. Renders Plant Health Report, Highlighted Overlay, Symptom Bars, Care Plan & History Chart

2. Answering the #1 Viva Question: "Why Did the Model Train in Under 1 Second Instead of Hours?"

Most students assume every image AI project has to train a heavy Deep Learning CNN (like ResNet or MobileNetV2) on 50,000+ raw RGB images — which requires a GPU and takes hours.

For this Mini Project, we deliberately chose a Two-Stage Hybrid Architecture (Computer Vision Feature Extraction + Tabular Machine Learning), which is faster, explainable, and runs cleanly on any student laptop CPU:

Approach Input to Model Training Hardware & Time Explainability to Guide / Farmers
End-to-End CNN (e.g., MobileNetV2) Raw 224×224×3 pixels (150,528 values/image) GPU, 1–4 hours on 50k images Black box — hard to combine with soil/temp sensors
Our 2-Stage Pipeline (OpenCV + RandomForest) 11 structured numeric features (6 OpenCV leaf metrics + 5 sensor deviations) Standard laptop CPU, < 0.3 seconds 100% transparent — shows exact yellowing %, brown %, spot %, and sensor deviations

Why this is even better for our problem statement:

  1. Visual symptoms alone are ambiguous (yellowing can be caused by nitrogen deficiency or overwatering or heat). A pure image CNN cannot see soil moisture or air temperature.
  2. Stage 1 (OpenCV) converts any leaf photo into 6 deterministic botanical measurements in ~30 milliseconds — no training required for color/spot/contour math.
  3. Stage 2 (Scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier) trains 120 decision trees on 1,440 domain-calibrated agronomic feature rows (covering 7 stress classes across Crops, Garden Plants, and Trees) with 5-fold cross-validation in under a second on startup.
  4. How to scale with larger real datasets later: Whenever real labeled farm/garden data is collected (or PlantVillage images are processed through analyze_plant_image()), you simply append those rows to the training DataFrame — and we also included train_cnn_optional.py (MobileNetV2 transfer learning in TensorFlow/Keras) as an optional upgrade path if you expand to a full deep-learning ensemble later.

3. Complete Code Walkthrough (Show This in VS Code)

The entire backend is intentionally clean and modular — only 3 Python files + 1 frontend HTML file:

plant-stress-monitor/
├── app.py                  # FastAPI web server & REST API endpoints
├── engine.py               # OpenCV leaf analysis + Scikit-learn RandomForest engine
├── db.py                   # SQLite database (plants & scan history) + CSV export
├── static/
│   ├── index.html          # Responsive frontend UI (HTML + CSS + Vanilla JS)
│   └── logo.svg            # Project leaf brand logo
├── test_app.py             # Automated self-check test suite
└── requirements.txt        # Exact Python package list

A. engine.py — Computer Vision + Machine Learning Core

  1. PLANT_PROFILES dictionary

    • Stores species-specific ideal ranges (moisture, temp, humidity, light) for 12 plants across 3 categories:
      • Agricultural Crops: Tomato, Paddy (Rice), Chilli, Banana
      • Garden Plants: Rose, Hibiscus, Tulsi, Money Plant
      • Trees: Mango Tree, Coconut Palm, Neem Tree, General Plant

  2. _center_plant_frame(bgr, plant_mask) — Auto-Centering for Accuracy

    • Finds the bounding box (cv2.boundingRect) of the detected leaf pixels.
    • Crops tightly with a 14% margin and places the leaf dead-center on a standardized 480×360 canvas.
    • Result: Even if a user uploads an off-center phone photo, measurements stay consistent and accurate.

  3. analyze_plant_image(image_bytes) — OpenCV Symptom Extraction

    • Converts image from BGR → HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) and CIE-Lab (Lightness + color channels).
    • Plant Masking: Isolates organic plant hues (H: 5–95, S >= 28) and applies morphological closing (cv2.morphologyEx) so dark spots inside the leaf aren't excluded.
    • 6 Quantitative Visual Features:
      • green_pct: Healthy chlorophyll pixels (H: 36–88)
      • yellow_pct: Chlorosis / yellowing (H: 18–35, high brightness)
      • brown_pct: Necrosis / dry scorch (H: 4–20, lower brightness)
      • spot_pct: Fungal spots / lesions detected via local Lab lightness drop (local_mean_L - L > 24)
      • pale_pct: Bleaching / pale discoloration (low saturation, high brightness)
      • wilt_index: Contour solidity (area / convex_hull_area) + Canny edge density (cv2.Canny) to detect curling and wrinkling
    • Visual Overlay: Blends semi-transparent color masks onto the leaf (Yellow = Chlorosis, Red-Orange = Browning, Purple = Dark Spots, Green Contour = Leaf Boundary) and returns base64 JPEG images to the UI.

  4. PlantStressEngine — Scikit-learn Random Forest & Severity Fusion

    • Uses 11 features (6 visual + 5 environmental deltas: moisture_delta, temp_delta, humidity, light_delta, rain_wetness).
    • Trains RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=120, max_depth=12, random_state=42) and evaluates it using cross_val_score(..., cv=5).
    • Severity Score (0–100): Weighted fusion of visual and environmental stress: 
     severity_score = 0.58 * visual_stress + 0.42 * env_stress
  • Progression Tracking (Improving / Stable / Worsening): Compares the current severity_score with the plant's previous recorded observation:
    • Drop of >= 6 points → Improving
    • Increase of >= 6 points → Worsening
    • Within ±6 points → Stable

B. db.py — SQLite Persistence Layer

  • Uses Python's built-in sqlite3 (zero database installation needed on demo day!).
  • Two core tables:
    • plants (id, name, plant_type, category, zone, created_at)
    • observations (id, plant_id, timestamp, sensors_json, vision_json, stress_type, confidence, severity_score, severity_level, risk_level, trend, recommendations_json, overlay_b64)
  • On first startup, seeds 3 realistic demo plants (Tomato Crop, Terrace Hibiscus, Campus Mango Sapling) with multi-day history so the Plant History chart works immediately.

C. app.py — FastAPI REST Backend

Key endpoints you can show in VS Code (or test live at http://localhost:8000/docs):

Endpoint Method Purpose
/ GET Serves the web UI (static/index.html)
/api/analyze POST Runs OpenCV + RandomForest diagnosis, saves to SQLite, returns JSON + overlay
/api/plants GET / POST Lists all tracked plants or registers a new plant
/api/plants/{id}/history GET Returns full timeline + overall progression verdict for a plant
/api/plants/{id}/export.csv GET Downloads full plant history as a CSV file (compatible with Excel / MySQL / Firebase)
/api/sample-leaf/{kind} GET Generates clean OpenCV demo leaves (healthy, yellowing, drought, spotted)

D. static/index.html — Clean Zero-Framework Frontend

  • Pure HTML5 + CSS3 + Vanilla JavaScript (zero React/Node build tools required, loads instantly offline in college labs).
  • Webcam Capture: Uses browser navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia() + HTML5 snapshot.
  • Live Sensor Status Badges: Updates Ideal / Too Low / Too High pills in real time as sliders move relative to the chosen plant's profile.
  • Interactive SVG Trend Chart: Plots Stress Score (Red) vs. Healthy Green Area % (Green) over time with zero external charting libraries.

Step 4: Run the Application & Automated Tests

# Start the web server

Open http://localhost:8000 in Chrome or Edge! You can also open http://localhost:8000/docs to show the interactive FastAPI backend API documentation to your guide.

5. Top HOD Viva Questions & Crisp Answers

  1. Q: Why did you combine image analysis with environmental sensors instead of using only images? A: Multiple plant stresses (like nitrogen deficiency, overwatering, and heat stress) cause similar yellowing on leaves. Fusing OpenCV visual symptoms with soil moisture, temperature, humidity, light, and wetness lets the ML model separate the actual root cause accurately.
  2. Q: Why is Random Forest trained so quickly here? A: Because OpenCV handles raw image feature extraction deterministically (reducing hundreds of thousands of pixels into 6 botanical metrics), so the Random Forest only trains on 11 structured numerical features across 1,440 samples — taking under 0.3 seconds on CPU with high cross-validation accuracy.
  3. Q: How does the system detect whether a plant is improving or worsening? A: Every scan is stored in SQLite (observations table) linked to plant_id. On each new scan, engine.py compares the new severity score against the previous scan: a drop of 6+ points is marked **Improving, an increase of 6+ points is **Worsening, and within ±6 points is **Stable.
  4. Q: What happens if a user uploads an off-center leaf photo? A: _center_plant_frame() in engine.py detects the leaf contour bounding box, crops out excess background with a 14% margin, and re-centers the leaf on a standard 480×360 canvas before computing symptom percentages.
  5. Q: How do you export or migrate the database to MySQL / Firebase? A: All data logic is isolated inside db.py, and every plant has a one-click Export CSV endpoint (/api/plants/{id}/export.csv) that produces clean structured records ready for MySQL import, Firebase, or research analysis.

Backend.title: Hermes Agent Review 2026: The Self-Improving AI Agent
Backend.summary:
Most AI agents reset to zero every time you start a new conversation. Hermes Agent doesn't. Debugging code, writing articles, managing scheduled tasks across Telegram and Discord, and delegating parallel research workstreams all accumulate into the same persistent memory instead of evaporating at the end of each session. That learning loop isn't a gimmick — it's the single most differentiating feature in the personal AI agent space right now.

This review covers what Hermes Agent does, how its learning system actually works in practice, where it falls short, and whether it's worth your time in 2026.

If you want the short version: Hermes Agent is the best personal AI agent for power users who want an assistant that improves with use. It's not the easiest to set up, it doesn't support the most messaging platforms, and its documentation can be sparse in places. But if you value depth over breadth — an agent that remembers your preferences, builds skills from experience, and gets faster at your routine tasks — nothing else comes close.

What is Hermes Agent?

Hermes Agent is an open-source (MIT-licensed) personal AI agent built by Nous Research — the same team behind the Hermes family of LLMs. At 158K GitHub stars and 9,000+ commits, it's one of the most actively developed agent projects in the world.

The core proposition: an AI agent that grows with you. Unlike agents that treat every conversation as independent, Hermes builds persistent knowledge across sessions. It remembers what worked, creates reusable skills from complex tasks, searches its own conversation history, and develops an increasingly accurate model of who you are and how you work.

The project's homepage puts it well: "It's the only agent with a built-in learning loop — it creates skills from experience, improves them during use, nudges itself to persist knowledge, searches its own past conversations, and builds a deepening model of who you are across sessions."

Installation & Setup

One-Liner Install

On Linux, macOS, or WSL2:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

On Windows (PowerShell, early beta):

iex (irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.ps1)

The installer handles everything: uv, Python 3.11, Node.js, ripgrep, ffmpeg, and a portable Git Bash on Windows. No manual dependency wrangling.

After Installation

source ~/.bashrc # reload shell hermes # start chatting hermes setup # full setup wizard (provider, model, tools, channels) hermes model # choose your LLM hermes tools # configure tools hermes gateway # start messaging gateway

The setup wizard walks you through choosing a provider, configuring API keys, enabling tools, and connecting messaging platforms. It's not as hand-holding as OpenClaw's openclaw onboard wizard, but it covers everything you need.

Coming from OpenClaw?

Hermes has a built-in migration tool:

hermes claw migrate # Full interactive migration hermes claw migrate --dry-run # Preview what would be migrated hermes claw migrate --preset user-data # Migrate without secrets

This imports your SOUL.md, memories, skills, API keys, channel configs, and TTS assets. The migration is designed to move user data without carrying over secrets.

The Learning Loop: How Hermes Actually Gets Smarter

This is the feature that sets Hermes apart from every other agent. Let me break down each component and how it works in practice.

1. Persistent Memory with Periodic Nudges

Hermes maintains two memory stores:

  • MEMORY.md — the agent's own notes about the environment, tool quirks, project conventions, and lessons learned. Think of it as the agent's personal knowledge base. USER.md — a profile of who you are: communication preferences, coding style, recurring corrections, timezone, role. This is what makes the agent feel personalized.

The key detail: Hermes nudges itself to persist knowledge. After a session where you correct its approach or share a preference, the agent proactively saves it. You don't have to explicitly say "remember this." The next session, that knowledge is already loaded into context.

Example: After I corrected Hermes three times about using Chinese for communication, it saved a memory entry: "Communication language: always use Chinese." Now every new session starts in Chinese without prompting.

2. Automatic Skill Creation

After any complex task — defined as 5+ tool calls with reasoning between them — Hermes autonomously creates a skill. Skills are procedural memory: reusable step-by-step approaches for recurring task types.

Each skill is a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter (name, tags, version) and markdown body (trigger conditions, numbered steps, pitfalls, verification steps). They live in ~/.hermes/skills/.

Example: After a debugging session involving SSH tunnel setup and port forwarding, Hermes created a ssh-tunnel-debug skill. Next time I hit a similar issue, the skill fires automatically — with the exact commands and common pitfalls already documented.

3. Skill Self-Improvement

Skills aren't static. When Hermes uses a skill and encounters a step that's outdated, incomplete, or wrong, it patches the skill immediately. This means skills get better with use — they accumulate pitfalls, edge cases, and shortcuts that the initial creation couldn't anticipate.

This happens in practice: a skill that originally had 5 steps grows to 12 steps after a week of use, accumulating platform-specific workarounds, error handling, and verification steps nobody would have thought to document up front.

4. FTS5 Session Search

Hermes stores every conversation in a local SQLite database with FTS5 full-text search. When it encounters a new problem, it can search its own past conversations for relevant context — across sessions.

This means if you solved a similar problem three months ago, Hermes can find that conversation and apply the same approach. No other mainstream agent does this. OpenClaw has session history but no cross-session semantic recall. Claude Code and Codex treat every session as independent.

5. Honcho Dialectic User Modeling

Hermes integrates with Honcho, a dialectic user modeling system. This goes beyond simple preference storage — it builds a progressively deeper model of who you are: how you think, what you prioritize, how you communicate, what frustrates you.

In practice, this means Hermes adapts its communication style over time. If you prefer concise bullet-point answers, it learns to stop writing paragraphs. If you always ask follow-up questions about edge cases, it starts preemptively addressing them. The adaptation is gradual but noticeable after a few weeks.

Key Features

Multi-Platform Messaging

Hermes connects to 6 messaging platforms via its gateway: Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, and Email. You run hermes gateway setup to configure channels, then hermes gateway start to launch the gateway process. All platforms share conversation continuity — start a thread on Telegram, continue on Discord, and the agent remembers the full context.

This is fewer platforms than OpenClaw (24), but it covers the platforms that matter for most developers. The gateway also supports voice memo transcription — send a voice message on Telegram and Hermes transcribes and responds.

Terminal Interface

Hermes has a proper TUI (Terminal User Interface) with multiline editing, slash-command autocomplete, conversation history, interrupt-and-redirect, and streaming tool output. It's built with Python's Ink-inspired framework and feels like a modern terminal app, not a glorified REPL.

Key slash commands shared across CLI and messaging:

Action CLI Messaging
Start fresh /new or /reset /new or /reset
Change model /model provider:model /model provider:model
Set personality /personality name /personality name
Retry/undo /retry, /undo /retry, /undo
Compress context /compress /compress
Browse skills /skills /skill-name
Interrupt work Ctrl+C or new message /stop or new message
