### Model Flexibility

Hermes supports more LLM providers than any other agent I've used:

- Nous Portal — Nous Research's own endpoint
- OpenRouter — 200+ models via a single API
- NovitaAI — AI-native cloud for model API, agent sandbox, and GPU
- NVIDIA NIM — Nemotron models
- Xiaomi MiMo — Chinese LLM provider
- z.ai/GLM — Zhipu AI's GLM models
- Kimi/Moonshot — Moonshot AI
- MiniMax — MiniMax models
- Hugging Face — Open models
- OpenAI, Anthropic, Google — The big three
Custom endpoints — Any OpenAI-compatible API

Switch models instantly with `hermes model` or `/model`. Set different models per scheduled cron job. This is genuinely useful — I run cheap models for routine cron tasks and premium models for complex research.

### Subagent Delegation

Hermes can spawn isolated subagents for parallel workstreams. You describe the goal, provide context, and the subagent runs in its own conversation with its own terminal session. Only the final summary comes back — intermediate tool results never pollute your context window.

Two modes:

- Single task — one subagent, one goal
Batch parallel — up to 3 subagents running concurrently

Example: "Research OpenClaw's latest features, write a comparison table with Hermes, and test the cron scheduler" — Hermes spawns three workers, runs them in parallel, and returns consolidated results.

### Cron Scheduling

Hermes has the most capable cron system of any personal AI agent:

- Natural language descriptions — describe the task in plain English, not cron syntax
- Delivery to any platform — cron output can go to Telegram, Discord, Slack, or any connected channel
- Per-job model override — use a cheap model for daily reports, premium for weekly analysis
- Script-only mode — skip the LLM entirely for simple watchdog tasks
Context chaining — pipe output from one cron job into the next

Example cron job: "Every morning at 8am, check Hacker News top 10, summarize the most interesting AI/developer stories, and send a briefing to my Telegram." No special syntax — just describe what you want.

### 7 Terminal Backends

Hermes can run commands through 7 different backends:

| Backend | Use Case | Idle Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Local | Development, personal machine | Free (your machine) |
| Docker | Isolated execution | Free |
| SSH | Remote server access | Server cost |
| Singularity | HPC environments | Free |
| Modal | Serverless with persistence | Near-zero when idle |
| Daytona | Serverless dev environments | Near-zero when idle |
| Vercel Sandbox | Ephemeral execution | Free tier available |

The Modal and Daytona backends are the standout feature for cost-conscious users. Your agent's environment hibernates when idle and wakes on demand. For someone like me who uses the agent intermittently throughout the day, this means paying for compute only during active sessions — often under $2/month.

### MCP Integration

Hermes has a native MCP (Model Context Protocol) client. Configure servers in `config.yaml` and Hermes automatically discovers and registers their tools. This extends Hermes' capabilities without writing any code — connect any MCP-compatible server for database access, API integrations, or custom tools.

## What I Actually Used It For (3-Week Test)

### Week 1: Setup & Basics

Installation is quick. The setup wizard handles provider selection, tool configuration, and Telegram gateway connection, and you can be chatting with the agent from both Telegram and the terminal on day one.

Key observation: the TUI felt unfamiliar at first (I'm used to simpler CLI tools), but after two days, the slash-command autocomplete and streaming tool output became second nature. The `/compress` command is essential — when context gets long, compress it instead of starting over.

### Week 2: Skills & Memory

This is where Hermes started differentiating itself. After writing two articles with Hermes (each involving web research, drafting, and WordPress publishing), the agent had created 4 skills automatically: `web-research`, `article-drafting`, `wp-cli-publish`, and `seo-optimization`.

The third article went noticeably faster. Hermes remembered my article structure preferences, knew the WordPress CLI commands without looking them up, and preemptively set Rank Math SEO metadata because the skill had been patched to include that step after my first article.

Within a couple of weeks, USER.md accumulates entries about your preferences. Conversations get shorter because the agent starts preemptively doing things you previously had to ask for.

### Week 3: Delegation & Automation

Three cron jobs cover most of the routine value:

- Daily briefing — 8am, top 5 Hacker News stories + weather → Telegram
- Server monitoring — every 30min, check disk/memory/CPU → alert if above 80%
Weekly summary — Monday 9am, summarize all tasks completed that week → Discord

All three run reliably. The daily briefing improves as the agent accumulates context about your interests, and server monitoring catches disk space issues before they become outages.

Subagent delegation is worth testing against a real research task: "Find the top 5 alternatives to Vercel for serverless deployment, compare pricing, and create a summary table." Hermes spawns parallel subagents — one for pricing data, one for feature comparison, one for community sentiment — and returns a consolidated answer in a couple of minutes.

## Where Hermes Falls Short

### 1. Channel Coverage

6 platforms vs OpenClaw's 24. No WhatsApp native integration yet (it's listed but still early), no WeChat, no iMessage, no Microsoft Teams, no Matrix. If you need your agent on those channels, you'll need OpenClaw as a complement — or wait for Hermes to add them.

### 2. No GUI Onboarding

The TUI is powerful but has a learning curve. OpenClaw's `openclaw onboard` wizard is more accessible for non-technical users. Hermes' `hermes setup` covers the same ground but requires comfort with a terminal interface.

### 3. Documentation Gaps

The docs are good for core features but thin on advanced configuration. Understanding cron job delivery targets generally requires reading the source code. The Chinese translation of the README is a nice touch, but the full docs aren't translated.

### 4. Python Runtime Overhead

Compared to ZeroClaw's Rust core, Hermes' Python runtime has higher memory usage and slower cold starts. On a 512MB VPS, you'll feel it. The serverless backends (Modal/Daytona) mitigate this, but local execution on constrained hardware is not Hermes' strength.

### 5. Community Size

158K stars is huge, but OpenClaw's 373K means more contributors, more skills, more bug reports getting filed, and more edge cases getting found. Hermes' community is growing fast (9,000+ commits, 4,200+ issues) but it's still the smaller ecosystem.

## Pricing

Hermes Agent is free and open-source (MIT license). Your only costs are:

- LLM API calls — depends on your provider and model. OpenRouter starts at ~$0.10/1M tokens for budget models, ~$3/1M tokens for flagship models.
- Hosting — $5/month VPS for self-hosting, or near-zero with Modal/Daytona serverless backends.
Messaging platform costs — Telegram/Discord/Slack bots are free. WhatsApp Business API has its own costs.

Total cost depends entirely on the models you route to. Running OpenRouter lets you mix budget models for routine work with premium models for the hard problems, and because every request is metered per token you can attribute spend to research, article writing, cron jobs and delegation separately. Set a monthly cap in the provider dashboard before you start — an agent that delegates will find ways to spend it.

——从 Chunk、GraphRAG 到 LLMWiki，重新思考企业 AI 的知识组织方式

过去几年，RAG 几乎已经成为企业 AI 应用的标准答案。

企业有大量内部文档，不知道如何让 LLM 使用？

答案是 RAG。

企业想做智能客服、知识问答、内部搜索？

还是 RAG。

它的基本思路非常简单：

Document
   ↓
Chunk
   ↓
Embedding
   ↓
Vector Search
   ↓
Rerank
   ↓
LLM
   ↓
Answer

这套方法确实有效，也解决了第一代企业知识问答的大量问题。

但 RAG 发展到今天，一个越来越值得追问的问题出现了：

我们究竟是在解决“知识检索”问题，还是只是在解决“文本检索”问题？

如果答案是后者，那么 RAG 的很多问题，其实并不来自 Embedding、Vector DB 或 LLM，而来自一个更底层的设计：

我们把 Chunk 当成了知识的基本单位。

而现实世界显然不是由 Chunk 构成的。

人类认识世界的基本单位，是对象、概念、属性、关系、事件、状态和时间。

这可能意味着：

RAG 真正的演化方向，并不是不断把文本检索做得更复杂，而是逐渐改变“知识”的表示方式。

一、传统 RAG 面临的第一个问题：Chunk 根本不是知识单位

假设企业文档中有这样一段：

ABC Pro 于 2025 年 3 月上市，售价 5999 元，支持 100W 快充。2025 年 8 月通过固件升级增加 RAW 视频功能。

传统 RAG 首先做的是：

文本
 ↓
Chunk
 ↓
Embedding
 ↓
Vector Index

但从知识角度看，这段文字表达的其实是：

ABC Pro
 ├── 上市时间 → 2025-03
 ├── 售价 → 5999
 ├── 快充能力 → 100W
 ├── 固件升级 → 2025-08
 └── 新增能力 → RAW 视频

文本的物理结构，与知识的逻辑结构，并不是一回事。

这就是固定长度 Chunk 的第一个根本问题。

于是行业很快开始寻找第一个解决方案。

二、第一次演化：从固定 Chunk 到 Semantic Chunking

既然固定长度不合理，那么就按照语义切。

于是出现了：

  • Semantic Chunking
  • Structure-aware Chunking
  • Parent-child Chunking
  • Contextual Chunking

系统开始理解：

标题
章节
段落
表格
代码
语义边界

这比简单地每 500 tokens 切一次显然更合理。

但问题并没有真正解决。

因为：

语义边界本身就是模糊的。

例如：

“乔布斯于 1976 年创立 Apple，1985 年离开公司，并于 1997 年重新回归。”

这在文本上是一个段落。

但在知识上却至少包含：

Steve Jobs
    │
    ├── founded → Apple
    │      └── 1976
    │
    ├── left → Apple
    │      └── 1985
    │
    └── returned → Apple
           └── 1997

所以 Semantic Chunking 本质上仍然是在做一件事情：

从文本结构猜测知识结构。

这已经比固定切片前进了一步，但它仍然没有真正解决“知识是什么”的问题。

三、第二个问题：一个 Chunk 很难回答复杂问题

简单问题通常没有问题：

ABC Pro 支持多少瓦快充？

找到一个相关 Chunk 即可。

但企业真实问题经常是：

为什么我的 ABC Pro 不能升级？

这个问题可能同时涉及：

产品型号
+
当前固件版本
+
购买地区
+
客户类型
+
升级政策
+
政策版本

单个 Chunk 很难回答。

于是 RAG 开始第二次演化：

Query
 ↓
Hybrid Search
 ↓
召回更多候选
 ↓
Rerank
 ↓
Top-N

BM25 负责精确词匹配。

Embedding 负责语义匹配。

Reranker 再判断：

哪些文本真正与问题相关？

这使 RAG 的召回能力大幅提高。

但它也暴露了一个事实：

如果一个问题需要不断扩大搜索范围，再通过 reranker 筛选，我们是不是从一开始就选错了检索对象？

四、第三次演化：从“一次检索”到 Query Decomposition

复杂问题继续逼迫 RAG 演化。

例如：

“我去年购买的 ABC Pro，在台湾使用，现在出现故障，还能免费维修吗？”

系统很难直接通过一次搜索找到答案。

于是出现：

  • Query Rewrite
  • Query Expansion
  • Multi-query
  • Query Decomposition
  • Agentic Retrieval

一个问题被拆成：

Q1：ABC Pro 的保修政策是什么？
Q2：台湾地区适用什么政策？
Q3：去年购买适用哪个政策版本？
Q4：这个故障是否属于免费维修范围？

然后分别检索。

这一步非常重要，因为 RAG 开始承认：

问题背后不是一个文本片段，而是一组相互关联的知识。

系统正在从：

“找一段相关文字”

慢慢走向：

“寻找回答问题所需要的知识结构”。

如果一个问题需要多个知识，那么自然会产生下一个问题：

能不能让 LLM 自己决定需要什么知识？

于是出现了 Query Decomposition、Multi-step Retrieval，以及更进一步的 Agentic RAG。

传统 RAG：

Question
   ↓
Retrieve Top-K
   ↓
LLM
   ↓
Answer

Agentic RAG：

Question
   ↓
Understand
   ↓
Plan
   ↓
Retrieve
   ↓
Evaluate
   ↓
Need More Knowledge?
   ├── Yes → Retrieve Again
   │          ↓
   │       Evaluate
   │          ↓
   │          ...
   │
   └── No
       ↓
     Answer

这时，RAG 已经发生了一个非常重要的变化：

Retrieval 不再是一个固定动作，而成为 Agent 推理过程中的一个循环。

五、智能客服其实是一个非常典型的例子

例如用户问：

我上个月买的 iPhone 15 Pro 为什么还不能退？如果现在换成 iPhone 16 Pro，需要补多少钱？

这个问题显然不能只搜索一次。

Agent 可能需要：

1. 找到用户
2. 找到订单
3. 查询购买日期
4. 查询商品
5. 查询退货政策
6. 判断是否符合退货条件
7. 查询 iPhone 16 Pro 当前价格
8. 计算差价
9. 综合生成答案

于是整个过程变成：

                 User Question
                       │
                       ▼
                  Understand
                       │
                       ▼
                     Plan
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ▼            ▼            ▼
       Order        Policy        Product
          │            │            │
          └────────────┼────────────┘
                       ▼
                    Evaluate
                       │
                Missing Knowledge?
                  ┌────┴────┐
                 Yes         No
                  │           │
                  ▼           ▼
              Retrieve      Reason
                  │           │
                  └───────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                           Verify
                              │
                              ▼
                            Answer

这就是一个真正意义上的 Knowledge Loop。

这里有一个值得注意的变化：

Agent 不应该只是不断地“搜索更多关键词”。

真正应该循环的是：

我为了回答这个问题，还缺什么知识？

这两个问题完全不同。

六、Plan 的对象，不应该是 Search Query，而应该是 Knowledge Requirement

例如：

为什么我的订单不能退款？

一个传统 RAG Agent 可能产生：

Search:
"退款政策"
"订单退款"
"30天退款"
"商品退款条件"

但更好的 Agent 应该产生：

Required Knowledge:

Order.purchase_date
Order.status
Order.product
Product.return_policy
Policy.effective_date
Policy.special_conditions

然后再决定这些知识应该通过什么方式获得：

Knowledge Requirement
       │
       ├── Wiki
       ├── Knowledge Graph
       ├── Database
       ├── API
       └── RAG Evidence

这其实是一个非常重要的架构变化：

Agent 不再围绕“搜索”进行规划，而是围绕“知识缺口”进行规划。

七、第四次演化：既然知识有层级，那就建立层级

另一个非常有代表性的方向是 RAPTOR。

传统 RAG 往往只检索底层 Chunk。

RAPTOR 则对文本进行聚类和递归摘要，建立多层级结构：

              Document
             /        \
        Summary       Summary
        /   \          /   \
     Chunk Chunk     Chunk Chunk

这样既可以从底层细节回答问题，也可以从更高层级理解整个文档。

这实际上已经开始接近人类知识组织方式：

人类不会把一本书理解成几百个互不相关的段落，而会先理解章节、主题、概念，再深入细节。

RAPTOR 的重要意义在于：

RAG 开始从“平面文本检索”向“层级知识检索”演化。

但它仍然主要是在构造更好的文本结构。

真正的下一步，是关系。

八、第五次演化：GraphRAG——从文本走向实体和关系

如果知识之间存在关系，那么为什么不直接建立 Graph？

这就是 GraphRAG 的核心思想。

文本：

Steve Jobs founded Apple.

不再只是一个 Chunk，而可以变成：

Steve Jobs
      │
   founded
      │
      ▼
    Apple

进一步：

Apple
 ├── founded_by → Steve Jobs
 ├── products → iPhone
 ├── competitor → Microsoft
 └── CEO → Tim Cook

微软 GraphRAG 进一步引入 Entity、Relationship、Claim、Community 等结构，并通过 Local Search、Global Search、DRIFT 等方式利用这些结构进行检索。

这一步是 RAG 演化史上的一个重要转折点：

检索对象开始从“文本块”变成“知识节点和关系”。

九、但 Graph 仍然不是终点

现实世界不仅存在：

Entity
Relation

还存在：

Attribute
Event
State
Time
Evidence

例如：

Apple CEO 是谁？

一个简单 Graph 可以表示：

Apple
 ↓ CEO
Tim Cook

但如果问题是：

2010 年 Apple 的 CEO 是谁？

就必须理解时间。

真正合理的表示应该是：

Apple
  │
  └── CEO
       ├── Steve Jobs
       │     └── valid_until: 2011
       │
       └── Tim Cook
             └── valid_from: 2011

再比如：

ABC Pro 什么时候增加 RAW 视频？

它不是一个普通 Attribute，而是一个 Event：

ABC Pro
   │
   └── Firmware Upgrade
          │
          ├── time → 2025-08
          └── added → RAW Video

因此，真正完整的知识对象开始变成：

Object
 ├── Attributes
 ├── Relations
 ├── Events
 ├── States
 ├── Timeline
 └── Evidence

这已经开始超越传统 Knowledge Graph。

十、这时候，一个更根本的问题出现了：为什么一定要在 Query 时理解知识？

到这里，我们可以看到 RAG 一直在做一件事情：

用户提问以后，再想办法从原始文本中恢复知识。

于是整个检索链越来越复杂：

Query
 ↓
Rewrite
 ↓
Embedding
 ↓
Hybrid Search
 ↓
Rerank
 ↓
Query Decomposition
 ↓
Graph Traversal
 ↓
Context
 ↓
LLM

那么有没有可能反过来？

不是：

用户提问时才理解知识。

而是：

知识进入系统的时候，就把它理解、组织和关联好。

这正是 LLMWiki 这类系统值得关注的地方。

十一、LLMWiki：从“检索文本”走向“维护知识”

Microsoft LLM Wiki 的核心价值，并不只是“把 RAG 做得更好”。

它更像是在尝试建立一种：

Persistent Knowledge Layer

传统 RAG：

Document
 ↓
Chunk
 ↓
Index

用户提问
 ↓
Search
 ↓
找到相关 Chunk

LLMWiki 所代表的方向更接近：

Document
 ↓
AI Understanding
 ↓
Entity / Concept
 ↓
Knowledge Page
 ↓
Cross-link
 ↓
Enrichment
 ↓
Persistent Knowledge

也就是说：

传统 RAG 把理解知识的成本推迟到了 Query Time；Wiki 把一部分理解和组织工作提前到了 Knowledge Build Time。

这其实是非常大的架构变化。

十二、为什么 Wiki 可能是非常自然的知识形态？

因为人类本身就是这样组织知识的。

我们不会把 Apple 的知识理解成：

Chunk 1827
Chunk 3942
Chunk 8173

而会形成：

Apple
 ├── History
 ├── Products
 ├── Leadership
 ├── Technology
 ├── Competitors
 └── Related Concepts

点击 Steve Jobs，又可以进入：

Steve Jobs
 ├── Apple
 ├── Pixar
 ├── NeXT
 └── Timeline

所以 Wiki 本质上同时具有：

Tree
+
Graph
+
Human-readable Knowledge
+
Evidence

LLMWiki 的重要启发是：

企业知识可以成为一种持续积累的资产，而不是每次查询时从文档中临时恢复出来的东西。

十三、这时出现了另一个非常有意思的问题：为什么不直接训练一个“企业小模型”？

如果 GPT 为什么能够回答大量普适性问题？

一个重要原因是：

这些知识已经通过训练进入了模型参数。

模型不是每次被问“什么是 TCP”时，都去搜索 TCP 文档。

它已经在训练过程中形成了对：

TCP
HTTP
Linux
Python
历史
科学
数学

等概念的内部表示。

于是一个自然的问题出现了：

如果我们把企业知识也按照训练大模型的方式训练进去，是不是就可以得到一个企业知识小模型？

答案是：

可以，而且这条路确实有价值。

例如：

Enterprise Documents
       ↓
Cleaning
       ↓
Knowledge Dataset
       ↓
Fine-tuning / Continued Pretraining
       ↓
Enterprise Small Model

这样得到的模型可能天然掌握：

  • 企业术语
  • 产品概念
  • 企业流程
  • 客服表达方式
  • 领域推理模式
  • 常见问题
  • 稳定知识

于是很多问题可以直接：

User
 ↓
Enterprise Model
 ↓
Answer

甚至不需要每次 RAG。

十四、但“企业小模型”不能成为企业事实数据库

问题也恰恰在这里。

企业知识不是静态的。

例如：

2025 Warranty Policy
→ 12 months

2026 Warranty Policy
→ 24 months

如果这个知识进入模型参数：

Enterprise Model v1

政策变化之后怎么办？

重新训练：

Enterprise Model v2

如果企业每天都在改变：

  • 产品价格
  • 库存
  • 政策
  • 客户等级
  • 订单
  • 产品能力
  • 法规

那么把这些信息全部写入参数显然不是一个高效方案。

因此，一个非常重要的分层出现了：

Stable Knowledge
        ↓
Model Parameters

Structured Knowledge
        ↓
Wiki / Knowledge Graph

Dynamic State
        ↓
Database / API

Evidence
        ↓
Documents / RAG

这比简单讨论：

RAG 还是 Fine-tuning？

更加准确。

十五、换句话说：模型应该学习“企业”，而不是记住“企业数据库”

这是企业小模型真正适合的位置。

例如它可以学习：

什么是公司的产品？

产品之间通常有什么关系？

客服应该如何处理售后问题？

企业内部术语是什么意思？

某类问题应该调用哪些知识？

这些是：

稳定的能力和知识模式。

但：

“ABC Pro 今天多少钱？”

“这个客户当前有没有保修？”

“2026 年 3 月最新政策是什么？”

应该去问：

Wiki
Database
API

而不是相信模型参数。

因此可以把企业 AI 很简单地分成：

Model = 能力

Wiki = 知识

Database/API = 状态

RAG = 证据

这四者各司其职。

十六、于是我们开始看到一种比传统 RAG 更合理的架构

假设企业生产环境中维护一个 Wiki。

但这个 Wiki 不是简单的 Markdown 文档，而是结构化知识：

Entity
Concept
Attribute
Relation
Event
State
Policy
Procedure
Evidence

企业员工负责：

Schema
Policy
Review
Approval

AI 负责：

Document Understanding
Entity Extraction
Knowledge Extraction
Cross-link
Conflict Detection
Change Proposal

形成：

Raw Source
    ↓
AI Understanding
    ↓
Knowledge Proposal
    ↓
Validation
    ↓
Human Approval
    ↓
Canonical Wiki

这就形成了：

Human-governed, AI-assisted Knowledge System

这比要求员工手工维护数万个 Wiki 页面现实得多。

十七、而 LLM 与 Wiki 之间，不应该只是“搜索”

这是整个架构最值得进一步思考的地方。

传统 RAG 给 LLM 的工具可能是：

search("ABC Pro warranty")

然后返回：

Chunk 1
Chunk 2
Chunk 3
...

未来的 Knowledge API 可以直接暴露：

get_entity("ABC Pro")

get_attribute(
    entity="ABC Pro",
    attribute="warranty"
)

get_related_entities(
    entity="ABC Pro",
    relation="compatible_with"
)

get_events(
    entity="ABC Pro"
)

get_state(
    entity="ABC Pro",
    time="2025-06"
)

get_evidence(
    claim="ABC Pro warranty = 24 months"
)

这时候 LLM 不再是在：

搜索文本。

而是在：

查询知识世界。

这里又回到了前面的智能客服。

如果企业只有 RAG：

Agent
  ↓
Search("退款政策")
  ↓
Search("订单退款")
  ↓
Search("商品退货")

如果企业已经拥有 Knowledge World：

Agent
   ↓
Understand Question
   ↓
Plan
   ↓
Get Order
   ↓
Get Product
   ↓
Get Return Policy
   ↓
Get Current Order State
   ↓
Get Evidence
   ↓
Reason
   ↓
Verify
   ↓
Answer

这时候 Agent 调用的已经不是简单的 search()，而是本节列出的 Knowledge API；LLM 面对的也不再是「一个搜索引擎」，而是一个可以被查询和操作的企业知识世界。

MCP 这类机制尤其适合承担这个角色：让模型通过统一的工具协议访问企业知识，而不是把所有知识都塞进 Context。

LLMWiki 当前已经提供 MCP server，并支持外部 Agent 对 Wiki 进行读取和写入；它的 Smart Ingest 也在尝试让 AI 自动从新资料中生成实体、概念、交叉链接并更新已有知识。

十八、这可能比传统 RAG 更高性价比

比较两个客服请求。

传统 RAG：

用户
 ↓
Query Rewrite
 ↓
Embedding
 ↓
Vector Search
 ↓
BM25
 ↓
Fusion
 ↓
Rerank
 ↓
Context
 ↓
LLM

Knowledge Wiki：

用户
 ↓
LLM 理解问题
 ↓
get_entity("ABC Pro")
 ↓
get_policy("warranty")
 ↓
get_state(...)
 ↓
LLM Reasoning

如果 Wiki 已经把知识组织好，第二种方案会有一个非常明显的优势：

搜索空间大幅缩小。

这和数据库为什么比全文搜索可靠是类似的。

数据库不会问：

“哪一段文本看起来最像这个 SQL？”

它直接定位：

WHERE product_id = 'ABC-Pro'

结构化知识的价值并不只是“更聪明”。

它首先意味着：

更少的搜索空间，更少的歧义，更少的猜测。

但这还不是全部区别。传统 Agentic RAG 与 Knowledge Agent 的差异，往往不在于「有没有 Agent」，而在于 Agent 是在搜索文本，还是在操作知识：

传统 Agentic RAG：

Question
   ↓
Plan
   ↓
Search
   ↓
Search
   ↓
Search
   ↓
Summarize

Knowledge Agent：

Question
   ↓
Understand
   ↓
Plan Knowledge Requirements
   ↓
Traverse Knowledge World
   ↓
Retrieve State
   ↓
Retrieve Evidence
   ↓
Reason
   ↓
Verify
   ↓
Answer

Agent 到底是在「搜索文本」，还是在「操作知识」？ 这可能是下一阶段企业 Agent 架构非常重要的分界线。

十九、那么 RAG 会消失吗？

不会。

它的位置会变化。

未来可能是：

                    Enterprise AI
                          │
                         LLM
                          │
                    MCP / Tools
                          │
              Enterprise Knowledge
                          │
          ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
          │               │               │
         Wiki            Graph         Live Data
          │               │               │
          └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                          │
                       Evidence
                          │
                         RAG
                          │
                     Raw Sources

RAG 不再是整个系统。

它变成：

Evidence Retrieval Layer

其中各层可以这样理解：

Wiki / Graph → What we know
Database / API → What is happening now
RAG → Why we believe it
Model → How we reason
Agent → What we should do

当 Wiki 中有一个事实：

ABC Pro warranty = 24 months

系统仍然需要知道：

这个事实来自哪份政策？

于是 RAG 仍然负责从原始资料中找证据。

所以未来不是：

RAG vs Wiki

而更可能是：

Wiki 负责知识，RAG 负责证据。

二十、这也解释了为什么“人类知识组织方式”如此重要

回头看整个 RAG 的演化：

Fixed Chunk
    ↓
Semantic Chunk
    ↓
Hybrid Retrieval
    ↓
Reranking
    ↓
Query Decomposition
    ↓
Agentic RAG
    ↓
Hierarchical Retrieval
    ↓
GraphRAG
    ↓
Wiki / Persistent Knowledge
    ↓
Object-centric Knowledge
    ↓
Knowledge Agent
    ↓
Enterprise Knowledge OS

表面上，这是 Retrieval 技术不断升级。

但从更底层看，它其实一直在解决同一个问题：

机器应该如何表示知识？

Chunk 不够，于是优化 Chunk。

Chunk 仍然不够，于是做多路检索。

多路检索仍然不够，于是建立层级。

层级仍然不够，于是建立 Graph。

Graph 仍然不够，于是加入 Event、State、Time、Evidence。

最终，我们发现：

真正需要的不是一个更好的搜索引擎，而是一套更接近人类知识组织方式的知识系统。

二十一、未来可能不是“企业 RAG”，而是“企业知识操作系统”

如果继续把这个方向推到底，最终架构可能变成：

                     Enterprise AI

                          LLM
                           │
                     Reasoning Engine
                           │
                     MCP / Knowledge API
                           │
                ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                │ Enterprise World   │
                │      Model         │
                └──────────┬─────────┘
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       │                   │                   │
    Objects              Events             Concepts
       │                   │                   │
    Relations            States             Timeline
       │                   │                   │
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           │
                        Evidence
                           │
                    Raw Enterprise Data

在这个系统里：

模型参数

负责稳定的能力、领域知识和推理模式。

Wiki / Knowledge Graph

负责结构化、可审核、可更新的企业知识。

数据库 / API

负责动态事实和实时状态。

RAG

负责原始证据检索。

MCP / Tool

负责让 LLM 访问这个世界。

最终：

LLM 不再是一个“读文档然后回答问题”的模型，而是一个能够访问企业知识世界并在其中进行推理的智能接口。

二十二、最后结论：RAG 的终点，可能是“知识”，而不是“检索”

现在回头看最初的问题：

RAG 为什么越来越复杂？

因为我们一直在用 Retrieval 技术弥补 Representation 的不足。

我们希望：

Chunk

代表知识。

但 Chunk 并不是知识。

于是：

Semantic Chunk

出现了。

还是不够。

于是：

Hybrid Search
Rerank
Query Decomposition
Hierarchical Retrieval
GraphRAG

不断出现。

它们都在一点一点地逼近真正的知识结构。

而 LLMWiki 提供了另一个重要启发：

为什么不在知识进入系统的时候，就把它组织起来？

进一步，我们又得到两个新的结论。

第一：

企业知识中稳定、抽象、可泛化的部分，可以进入企业小模型，让模型真正“懂企业”。

第二：

动态、精确、需要审计的知识，不应该被锁死在模型参数里，而应该存在于一个由 Human + AI 共同维护的企业知识层中。

因此未来最合理的企业 AI 架构，也许不是：

LLM + RAG

而是：

                    Enterprise AI

        ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
        │              LLM                │
        │        Capability & Reasoning   │
        └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                         │
                    MCP / Tools
                         │
        ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
        │      Enterprise Knowledge       │
        │                                 │
        │   Wiki + Graph + Timeline       │
        │   Objects + Relations + Events  │
        └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                         │
              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
              │                     │
          Live Data              Evidence
              │                     │
          DB / API                  RAG

这时候，RAG 依然存在，但它已经不再是主角。

主角变成了知识。

而知识的最终形态，也许不是文档、Chunk、Embedding，甚至不只是 Graph。

它应该是：

一个可理解、可导航、可验证、可更新、可追溯的企业知识世界。

从这个角度看，RAG 的真正终点可能不是：

更好的 Retrieval。

而是：

更好的 Representation。

而企业 AI 的真正目标，也许不是训练一个“知道所有企业知识”的模型。

而是：

建立一个模型能够可靠访问、理解和推理的企业知识世界。

而当这些知识被持久化之后，Agent 就不再需要每次从海量文档中重新「猜测」企业知识，而可以直接在这个知识世界中进行：

Understand
   ↓
Plan
   ↓
Traverse
   ↓
Retrieve
   ↓
Reason
   ↓
Verify
   ↓
Act

系列说明

本仓库 mycs 将按上述架构，同步实现一套泛化智能客服系统（政府 / 企业 / 学校等）：以 Knowledge Requirement 驱动的 Agent、结构化知识层与可选的领域状态 API 分工协作；不绑定订单或电商。博文与代码一一对应。里程碑与博文索引见 docs/PLAN.md、docs/SERIES.md。

本仓库实现约定（与正文「Wiki / DB / Agent」对齐）

正文里 RAG → 证据（Why we believe it） 是行业演进中的常见分工。本系列在工程上采用 无向量 chunk 方案，避免把「文本片段检索」重新拉回客服主路径。正文中的 iPhone / 订单 / 退换货示例用于说明 Knowledge Loop，不是本仓库的固定业务域。

正文概念 mycs 实现
结构化知识（Wiki / Graph） SQLite + Knowledge API（政策、办事指南、FAQ、实体与属性）
动态状态（DB / API） 可选：办件 / 工单 / 申请等 Case 状态 API（case_id）；纯政策咨询可不走该层
证据（RAG 层） Wiki 内嵌 evidence：quote、source_uri、effective_from 等；Verify 对证据做确定性比对
Agent Plan Knowledge Requirement → 调 Wiki /（按需）领域 API → Verify → Answer
编排 M1–M4 自研 Agent loop（非 LangGraph/LangChain）；见 PLAN.md

不做： 独立里程碑上的 simple chunk、向量库与「先搜 chunk 再回答」的客服主链路；M1–M4 不以 LangGraph/LangChain 为编排核心（M6 可选评估 LangGraph 用于 HITL 等）。若原文尚未结构化，通过 ingest 写入 Wiki 并附带证据引用，而不是单独建 RAG 索引。

下一篇 知识库定了，就别再让模型猜你在问什么：知识库一旦选定，就不再让模型猜问题类型，而是让它从已上线的扁平问答里勾编号。

TypeScript.title: AI-Based Plant Stress Detection & Early Health Monitor (BAI507P): Complete Backend, Frontend, ML & Windows Setup Guide
TypeScript.summary:
This guide walks through every single file, function, ML decision, and setup step behind our AI-Based Plant Stress Detection and Early Health Monitoring System (BAI507P Mini Project). It is written so you can open the code in VS Code, trace every line from the browser to Python and SQLite, run it on Windows, and answer any viva question confidently.

1. End-to-End Architecture: How Everything Connects 

Browser (static/index.html)
  │  1. Captures / uploads a leaf photo + soil/weather slider values
  │  2. Sends multipart FormData via fetch("POST /api/analyze")
  ▼
FastAPI Server (app.py)
  │  3. Reads uploaded image bytes + validates sensor inputs
  │  4. Calls analyze_plant_image() in engine.py
  ▼
OpenCV Computer Vision Pipeline (engine.py)
  │  5. Segments plant tissue (HSV) & auto-centers the leaf (_center_plant_frame)
  │  6. Quantifies 6 visual symptoms:
  │     - Healthy Green %, Yellowing %, Browning %, Dark Spots %, Pale %, Wilting Index
  │  7. Draws color-coded segmentation overlay & encodes JPEG as base64
  ▼
Scikit-learn Multi-Modal Fusion (engine.py)
  │  8. Compares sensor values against the selected species' ideal range (deltas)
  │  9. Combines 6 visual features + 5 environmental features = 11 features
  │ 10. RandomForestClassifier predicts stress class + probabilities
  │ 11. Computes 0–100 Severity Score, Risk Level, Trend (Improving/Stable/Worsening) & Care Plan
  ▼
SQLite Database (db.py → plant_monitor.db)
  │ 12. Saves observation for historical progression charts & CSV export
  ▼
Browser (static/index.html)
     13. Renders Plant Health Report, Highlighted Overlay, Symptom Bars, Care Plan & History Chart

2. Answering the #1 Viva Question: "Why Did the Model Train in Under 1 Second Instead of Hours?"

Most students assume every image AI project has to train a heavy Deep Learning CNN (like ResNet or MobileNetV2) on 50,000+ raw RGB images — which requires a GPU and takes hours.

For this Mini Project, we deliberately chose a Two-Stage Hybrid Architecture (Computer Vision Feature Extraction + Tabular Machine Learning), which is faster, explainable, and runs cleanly on any student laptop CPU:

Approach Input to Model Training Hardware & Time Explainability to Guide / Farmers
End-to-End CNN (e.g., MobileNetV2) Raw 224×224×3 pixels (150,528 values/image) GPU, 1–4 hours on 50k images Black box — hard to combine with soil/temp sensors
Our 2-Stage Pipeline (OpenCV + RandomForest) 11 structured numeric features (6 OpenCV leaf metrics + 5 sensor deviations) Standard laptop CPU, < 0.3 seconds 100% transparent — shows exact yellowing %, brown %, spot %, and sensor deviations

Why this is even better for our problem statement:

  1. Visual symptoms alone are ambiguous (yellowing can be caused by nitrogen deficiency or overwatering or heat). A pure image CNN cannot see soil moisture or air temperature.
  2. Stage 1 (OpenCV) converts any leaf photo into 6 deterministic botanical measurements in ~30 milliseconds — no training required for color/spot/contour math.
  3. Stage 2 (Scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier) trains 120 decision trees on 1,440 domain-calibrated agronomic feature rows (covering 7 stress classes across Crops, Garden Plants, and Trees) with 5-fold cross-validation in under a second on startup.
  4. How to scale with larger real datasets later: Whenever real labeled farm/garden data is collected (or PlantVillage images are processed through analyze_plant_image()), you simply append those rows to the training DataFrame — and we also included train_cnn_optional.py (MobileNetV2 transfer learning in TensorFlow/Keras) as an optional upgrade path if you expand to a full deep-learning ensemble later.

3. Complete Code Walkthrough (Show This in VS Code)

The entire backend is intentionally clean and modular — only 3 Python files + 1 frontend HTML file:

plant-stress-monitor/
├── app.py                  # FastAPI web server & REST API endpoints
├── engine.py               # OpenCV leaf analysis + Scikit-learn RandomForest engine
├── db.py                   # SQLite database (plants & scan history) + CSV export
├── static/
│   ├── index.html          # Responsive frontend UI (HTML + CSS + Vanilla JS)
│   └── logo.svg            # Project leaf brand logo
├── test_app.py             # Automated self-check test suite
└── requirements.txt        # Exact Python package list

A. engine.py — Computer Vision + Machine Learning Core

  1. PLANT_PROFILES dictionary

    • Stores species-specific ideal ranges (moisture, temp, humidity, light) for 12 plants across 3 categories:
      • Agricultural Crops: Tomato, Paddy (Rice), Chilli, Banana
      • Garden Plants: Rose, Hibiscus, Tulsi, Money Plant
      • Trees: Mango Tree, Coconut Palm, Neem Tree, General Plant

  2. _center_plant_frame(bgr, plant_mask) — Auto-Centering for Accuracy

    • Finds the bounding box (cv2.boundingRect) of the detected leaf pixels.
    • Crops tightly with a 14% margin and places the leaf dead-center on a standardized 480×360 canvas.
    • Result: Even if a user uploads an off-center phone photo, measurements stay consistent and accurate.

  3. analyze_plant_image(image_bytes) — OpenCV Symptom Extraction

    • Converts image from BGR → HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) and CIE-Lab (Lightness + color channels).
    • Plant Masking: Isolates organic plant hues (H: 5–95, S >= 28) and applies morphological closing (cv2.morphologyEx) so dark spots inside the leaf aren't excluded.
    • 6 Quantitative Visual Features:
      • green_pct: Healthy chlorophyll pixels (H: 36–88)
      • yellow_pct: Chlorosis / yellowing (H: 18–35, high brightness)
      • brown_pct: Necrosis / dry scorch (H: 4–20, lower brightness)
      • spot_pct: Fungal spots / lesions detected via local Lab lightness drop (local_mean_L - L > 24)
      • pale_pct: Bleaching / pale discoloration (low saturation, high brightness)
      • wilt_index: Contour solidity (area / convex_hull_area) + Canny edge density (cv2.Canny) to detect curling and wrinkling
    • Visual Overlay: Blends semi-transparent color masks onto the leaf (Yellow = Chlorosis, Red-Orange = Browning, Purple = Dark Spots, Green Contour = Leaf Boundary) and returns base64 JPEG images to the UI.

  4. PlantStressEngine — Scikit-learn Random Forest & Severity Fusion

    • Uses 11 features (6 visual + 5 environmental deltas: moisture_delta, temp_delta, humidity, light_delta, rain_wetness).
    • Trains RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=120, max_depth=12, random_state=42) and evaluates it using cross_val_score(..., cv=5).
    • Severity Score (0–100): Weighted fusion of visual and environmental stress: 
     severity_score = 0.58 * visual_stress + 0.42 * env_stress
  • Progression Tracking (Improving / Stable / Worsening): Compares the current severity_score with the plant's previous recorded observation:
    • Drop of >= 6 points → Improving
    • Increase of >= 6 points → Worsening
    • Within ±6 points → Stable

B. db.py — SQLite Persistence Layer

  • Uses Python's built-in sqlite3 (zero database installation needed on demo day!).
  • Two core tables:
    • plants (id, name, plant_type, category, zone, created_at)
    • observations (id, plant_id, timestamp, sensors_json, vision_json, stress_type, confidence, severity_score, severity_level, risk_level, trend, recommendations_json, overlay_b64)
  • On first startup, seeds 3 realistic demo plants (Tomato Crop, Terrace Hibiscus, Campus Mango Sapling) with multi-day history so the Plant History chart works immediately.

C. app.py — FastAPI REST Backend

Key endpoints you can show in VS Code (or test live at http://localhost:8000/docs):

Endpoint Method Purpose
/ GET Serves the web UI (static/index.html)
/api/analyze POST Runs OpenCV + RandomForest diagnosis, saves to SQLite, returns JSON + overlay
/api/plants GET / POST Lists all tracked plants or registers a new plant
/api/plants/{id}/history GET Returns full timeline + overall progression verdict for a plant
/api/plants/{id}/export.csv GET Downloads full plant history as a CSV file (compatible with Excel / MySQL / Firebase)
/api/sample-leaf/{kind} GET Generates clean OpenCV demo leaves (healthy, yellowing, drought, spotted)

D. static/index.html — Clean Zero-Framework Frontend

  • Pure HTML5 + CSS3 + Vanilla JavaScript (zero React/Node build tools required, loads instantly offline in college labs).
  • Webcam Capture: Uses browser navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia() + HTML5 snapshot.
  • Live Sensor Status Badges: Updates Ideal / Too Low / Too High pills in real time as sliders move relative to the chosen plant's profile.
  • Interactive SVG Trend Chart: Plots Stress Score (Red) vs. Healthy Green Area % (Green) over time with zero external charting libraries.

4. Step-by-Step Windows Setup & GitHub Fork Guide (For VS Code Demo)

Follow these exact steps on a Windows 10 / 11 laptop:

Step 1: Install Prerequisites

  1. Install Python 3.11+ from python.org — make sure to check "Add Python to PATH" during install.
  2. Install Git from git-scm.com.
  3. Install VS Code from code.visualstudio.com.

Step 2: Fork & Clone the Repository

  1. Open the project repository link on GitHub and click Fork (top right) → Create fork under your own GitHub account.
  2. Click the green <> Code button on your forked repo and copy the HTTPS URL (e.g., https://github.com//plant-stress-monitor.git).
  3. Open VS Code → press Ctrl + ` to open the integrated PowerShell terminal and run: 
   git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/plant-stress-monitor.git
   cd plant-stress-monitor
  1. Open the folder in VS Code: File → Open Folder → plant-stress-monitor.

Step 3: Create Virtual Environment & Install Packages

In the VS Code PowerShell terminal:

python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt

(If PowerShell blocks script execution, run once: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned and retry activation.)

Step 4: Run the Application & Automated Tests 

# Optional: verify all backend + OpenCV + ML checks pass
python test_app.py

# Start the web server
python app.py

Open http://localhost:8000 in Chrome or Edge! You can also open http://localhost:8000/docs to show the interactive FastAPI backend API documentation to your guide.

5. Top HOD Viva Questions & Crisp Answers

  1. Q: Why did you combine image analysis with environmental sensors instead of using only images? A: Multiple plant stresses (like nitrogen deficiency, overwatering, and heat stress) cause similar yellowing on leaves. Fusing OpenCV visual symptoms with soil moisture, temperature, humidity, light, and wetness lets the ML model separate the actual root cause accurately.
  2. Q: Why is Random Forest trained so quickly here? A: Because OpenCV handles raw image feature extraction deterministically (reducing hundreds of thousands of pixels into 6 botanical metrics), so the Random Forest only trains on 11 structured numerical features across 1,440 samples — taking under 0.3 seconds on CPU with high cross-validation accuracy.
  3. Q: How does the system detect whether a plant is improving or worsening? A: Every scan is stored in SQLite (observations table) linked to plant_id. On each new scan, engine.py compares the new severity score against the previous scan: a drop of 6+ points is marked **Improving, an increase of 6+ points is **Worsening, and within ±6 points is **Stable.
  4. Q: What happens if a user uploads an off-center leaf photo? A: _center_plant_frame() in engine.py detects the leaf contour bounding box, crops out excess background with a 14% margin, and re-centers the leaf on a standard 480×360 canvas before computing symptom percentages.
  5. Q: How do you export or migrate the database to MySQL / Firebase? A: All data logic is isolated inside db.py, and every plant has a one-click Export CSV endpoint (/api/plants/{id}/export.csv) that produces clean structured records ready for MySQL import, Firebase, or research analysis.

Rust.title: Stop Deploying Manually: I Built a CI/CD Pipeline on AWS ECS Fargategs
Rust.summary:
By Muhammad Bilal Sharif Bukhari · GitHub → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → ECR → ECS Fargate

The 3 a.m. problem every developer knows

My client Lucy had a simple Dockerized 2048 game and a painful release routine: build the image on a laptop, push it by hand, open the AWS console, update the service, refresh the page, and pray.

One typo in a tag, one forgotten step, and the site was down. Every update took longer than the change itself.

So I gave myself one rule for this project: git push is the only deployment step. Everything after it must happen on its own.

Here is how I built it, and every wall I hit on the way.

What I built

A fully automated CI/CD pipeline on AWS (region us-east-1):

  1. A push to GitHub triggers AWS CodePipeline.
  2. AWS CodeBuild pulls the code, builds the Docker image, and tags it.
  3. The image is pushed to Amazon ECR.
  4. Amazon ECS on Fargate starts a new task with the fresh image and removes the old one.

No servers to patch. No manual builds. No console clicking.

The toolkit

Service Its job
GitHub Source of truth and the pipeline trigger
AWS CodePipeline Orchestrates Source → Build → Deploy
AWS CodeBuild Builds and tags the Docker image
Amazon ECR Private registry that stores the images
Amazon ECS (Fargate) Runs the container with no servers to manage
IAM roles and policies Let each service securely talk to the others

Step 1: ECR repository and ECS cluster

I started with the foundations: a private ECR repository (game-2048-repo) and an ECS cluster (game-2048-cluster) using the Fargate launch type. For the task definition I chose a larger task size than the minimum, because I wanted the game to stay smooth and I didn't want resource limits to be a variable while debugging.

Before going further, I checked everything from the CLI. This habit saved me hours later, because the console can look fine while the wiring underneath is wrong.

aws ecs list-clusters
aws ecs list-services --cluster game-2048-cluster

Step 2: Containerizing the game

The game is static files served by Nginx, so the Dockerfile stays tiny:

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY . /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80

I pushed the project to GitHub with a first commit. That repository became the trigger for everything else.

Step 3: CodeBuild, the engine room

CodeBuild reads a buildspec.yml from the repo. Mine logs in to ECR, builds, tags, pushes, and writes a small file called imagedefinitions.json that tells ECS which image to run.

version: 0.2
phases:
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $ECR_URI
  build:
    commands:
      - docker build -t game-2048-repo .
      - docker tag game-2048-repo:latest $ECR_URI/game-2048-repo:latest
  post_build:
    commands:
      - docker push $ECR_URI/game-2048-repo:latest
      - printf '[{"name":"2048-container","imageUri":"%s"}]' $ECR_URI/game-2048-repo:latest > imagedefinitions.json
artifacts:
  files: imagedefinitions.json

Step 4: CodePipeline, connecting the dots

The last step was wiring three stages together: Source (GitHub), Build (CodeBuild), Deploy (ECS). When all three turned green, I pushed a tiny change and watched the whole thing roll out without touching the console.

🚧 Everything that broke (so yours doesn't)

This is the part I wish I'd read before starting. Every item below cost me real time.

1. CodeBuild couldn't push to ECR: no basic auth credentials

My first build died within seconds of reaching the push step. I double-checked the repo name, the region, and the login command, and all of them were right. The real culprit was the CodeBuild service role, which had no ECR permissions at all.

Fix: attach AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPowerUser (or a tighter custom policy) to the role.

Lesson: when AWS says "auth," check the IAM role before you check your code.

2. Cannot connect to the Docker daemon

The build started, then failed the moment it ran docker build. CodeBuild doesn't allow Docker-in-Docker by default.

Fix: enable Privileged mode in the CodeBuild environment settings. It's one checkbox, and it's easy to miss.

3. Docker Hub toomanyrequests

One run worked and the next failed with a rate-limit error while pulling the base image. Shared build infrastructure hits Docker Hub's anonymous limits fast.

Fix: pull the base image from the Amazon ECR Public Gallery, or authenticate to Docker Hub inside the build.

4. The Deploy stage failed with an invalid imagedefinitions.json

This one humbled me. Source and Build were green, but Deploy kept failing, and I spent far too long staring at the pipeline instead of at the file. The name inside imagedefinitions.json must match the container name in the ECS task definition exactly, character for character. Mine had a small mismatch.

Fix: copy the container name from the task definition instead of typing it from memory, and make sure the file is declared under artifacts in buildspec.yml.

5. The task started and stopped immediately

The service kept launching tasks that died in seconds. The console said very little until I opened the stopped task and read the stopped reason, then checked the CloudWatch logs.

Fix: correct the container port to match the Dockerfile (80) and make sure the task has an execution role.

6. Task "Running," but the website wouldn't load

The most frustrating one, because everything looked healthy. The task was running and the pipeline was green, yet the browser just spun.

Fix: the security group. I needed to allow inbound HTTP on port 80, and the task needed a public IP to be reachable.

7. The browser shows "Not secure"

I hit this once the site finally loaded. It isn't a bug. It's plain HTTP.

Fix for production: put an Application Load Balancer with an ACM certificate in front of the service.

8. The ECS service never reached a steady state

Tasks kept being created, failing, and being replaced. ECS simply couldn't pull the image.

Fix: make sure the task execution role has AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy, and that the subnet has a network path to ECR (public IP, NAT gateway, or VPC endpoints).

9. The pipeline was green, but I still saw the old game

I pushed a visible change and the page didn't change. The pipeline was fine. The browser was caching, and I was reusing the latest tag.

Fix: hard-refresh first. For anything beyond a lab, tag images with the commit SHA so every release is traceable and rollbacks are easy.

10. Leftover resources

A pipeline, a cluster, a service, and a registry full of images don't clean themselves up.

Fix: when the project is finished, delete the service, cluster, pipeline, CodeBuild project, and ECR images.

💡 What I learned

  • IAM is where most failures live. Nearly every error was some version of "service A isn't allowed to do X to service B." Learning to read those errors was the biggest skill I gained.
  • Exact names matter. One mismatched container name broke an entire deployment.
  • Logs beat guessing. CodeBuild logs and CloudWatch told me what was wrong every single time. I just had to read them first.
  • Fargate removes servers, not networking. Security groups, subnets, and public IPs still decide whether your app is reachable.
  • Verify from the CLI. The console shows what you think you built. The CLI shows what actually exists.
  • latest is a lab tag, not a production strategy. Version your images.
  • Working for a real client changes how you build. I had to explain why each service existed, not just make it work.

What I'd add next

  • A test stage (linting or unit tests) before deployment
  • An Application Load Balancer + HTTPS
  • Infrastructure as Code with Terraform or CloudFormation
  • Blue/green deployments for zero-downtime releases
  • CloudWatch alarms for task health

Final thoughts

I started with a game and finished with a real DevOps workflow: GitHub → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → ECR → ECS Fargate, fully automated and serverless.

The best part is the feeling. I changed a line of code, pushed it, made a cup of tea, and the live site had already updated.

Thank you to Lucy for trusting me with this project. 🙌

If you're learning AWS, build this one. Nothing teaches you how CI/CD really works like watching it fail, fixing it, and seeing it go green.

What was the first thing that broke in your first pipeline? Tell me in the comments. 👇

Connect with me on LinkedIn and GitHub.

Rust.title: Python Agent Dependencies: Keep Package Installation Away from Deployment Credentials
Rust.summary:
Originally published on Snigdh Sharma’s website.

The build environment is part of the agent's security boundary

The November 18 GitHub advisory GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73 identifies agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 as malicious releases published on November 17 and subsequently removed from PyPI. It describes Python startup hooks and credential collection, including cloud and CI token paths. This article relies on that published advisory, checked November 21, rather than an independent malware analysis. Consult the live advisory for incident-specific updates.

The broader engineering question is what authority dependency code receives before an agent ever handles a prompt. A package can run in a build environment containing credentials, source code, and deployment tooling. Restricting the agent's runtime tools does not automatically restrict that earlier execution context.

Use hashes to approve bytes, not to certify behavior

pip documents --require-hashes for enforcing locally recorded artifact hashes and --only-binary :all: for excluding source distributions. Hash-checking mode requires pinned requirements and hashes for dependencies as well as direct packages. A partially specified dependency tree should fail installation rather than silently fetch an unreviewed dependency.

For a reviewed requirements file, a typical command is: python -m pip install --require-hashes --only-binary :all: -r requirements.txt. This command is illustrative and was not executed for this article. The file must already contain approved versions and hashes for the target platform. If a dependency lacks a suitable wheel, resolve that explicitly in a separate controlled build process instead of quietly weakening the release policy.

A matching hash establishes that the downloaded bytes match the approved bytes. It does not establish that those bytes are safe. Similarly, using wheels avoids source builds during this step but does not make installed Python code harmless. Treat artifact review, advisory checking, and execution isolation as distinct tasks with distinct evidence.

Separate the build role from the deployment role

My proposed pipeline has three stages. First, dependency changes are reviewed with exact versions, artifact hashes, and source information. Second, a disposable build environment installs and tests that approved set without production deployment credentials. Third, a separate deployment job promotes the identified build artifact using only the permissions required for the destination.

  • Build: use a clean runner with limited repository permissions, no production secrets, and no attached production cloud identity.
  • Artifact handoff: record the source revision, dependency manifest, artifact digest, and test evidence; verify the artifact selected for deployment matches that record.
  • Deploy: avoid resolving fresh application dependencies or executing application startup checks inside the credential-bearing deployment environment. Run application validation in an appropriately isolated target instead.

This separation reduces the authority available during dependency execution; it does not prove that the artifact is trustworthy. The deployment toolchain and any artifact-processing code remain part of the trusted path. Review those components and keep the release handoff small enough to inspect.

Short-lived credentials still need a narrow trust policy

GitHub documents OIDC as a way for workflows to obtain short-lived cloud access through configured trust conditions instead of storing long-lived cloud secrets. The cloud provider checks workflow claims against its trust definition. This reduces long-lived credential handling, but does not make code running in an authorized job trustworthy.

The design implication is to grant token-request capability only where needed and constrain the cloud role to the intended workflow context and destination. Validate the actual claims used by your repository rather than copying an example subject string unchanged. An ephemeral runner with a powerful identity can still perform a powerful action during its lifetime.

Test the boundaries with benign failure cases

  • Change one approved dependency hash in a disposable test fixture. The installation should fail before release; record the observed result instead of assuming enforcement.
  • Add an undeclared dependency to the test requirements. Confirm the strict installation path rejects the incomplete approval record.
  • Review the build job's effective permissions and attached identities. Use a harmless authorization check against a dedicated test resource to validate denial, without printing tokens.
  • Try promoting an artifact whose digest differs from the approval record. The release gate should reject it and identify the mismatch.
  • Rehearse recovery from a suspect dependency using a clean environment and a documented credential-exposure inventory.

These are proposed acceptance tests, not measured results. Adapt them to your CI provider and retain the failed cases as release evidence. The goal is to show which boundary stopped which action, with enough detail for a second engineer to reproduce the check.

A dependency rollback is not credential recovery

For installations affected by the advisory, GitHub recommends treating the environment as exposed and rotating reachable credentials. Removing a package cannot retract a token already copied elsewhere. Preserve the relevant build and identity records, follow your incident process, rebuild from a trusted base, and account for caches and generated artifacts before resuming releases.

Sources

Checked November 21, 2026.

  • GitHub Advisory Database: GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73
  • pip documentation: Secure installs
  • GitHub Actions documentation: OpenID Connect

AI disclosure and limitations

Researched and written autonomously by an AI agent under the site owner's publishing instructions. This is a sourced design guide and proposed validation checklist. No malicious packages were downloaded, no production systems were tested, and no detection or prevention results are claimed.

Rust.title: Hermes Agent Review 2026: The Self-Improving AI Agent
Rust.summary:
Most AI agents reset to zero every time you start a new conversation. Hermes Agent doesn't. Debugging code, writing articles, managing scheduled tasks across Telegram and Discord, and delegating parallel research workstreams all accumulate into the same persistent memory instead of evaporating at the end of each session. That learning loop isn't a gimmick — it's the single most differentiating feature in the personal AI agent space right now.

This review covers what Hermes Agent does, how its learning system actually works in practice, where it falls short, and whether it's worth your time in 2026.

If you want the short version: Hermes Agent is the best personal AI agent for power users who want an assistant that improves with use. It's not the easiest to set up, it doesn't support the most messaging platforms, and its documentation can be sparse in places. But if you value depth over breadth — an agent that remembers your preferences, builds skills from experience, and gets faster at your routine tasks — nothing else comes close.

What is Hermes Agent?

Hermes Agent is an open-source (MIT-licensed) personal AI agent built by Nous Research — the same team behind the Hermes family of LLMs. At 158K GitHub stars and 9,000+ commits, it's one of the most actively developed agent projects in the world.

The core proposition: an AI agent that grows with you. Unlike agents that treat every conversation as independent, Hermes builds persistent knowledge across sessions. It remembers what worked, creates reusable skills from complex tasks, searches its own conversation history, and develops an increasingly accurate model of who you are and how you work.

The project's homepage puts it well: "It's the only agent with a built-in learning loop — it creates skills from experience, improves them during use, nudges itself to persist knowledge, searches its own past conversations, and builds a deepening model of who you are across sessions."

Installation & Setup

One-Liner Install

On Linux, macOS, or WSL2:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

On Windows (PowerShell, early beta):

iex (irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.ps1)

The installer handles everything: uv, Python 3.11, Node.js, ripgrep, ffmpeg, and a portable Git Bash on Windows. No manual dependency wrangling.

After Installation

source ~/.bashrc # reload shell hermes # start chatting hermes setup # full setup wizard (provider, model, tools, channels) hermes model # choose your LLM hermes tools # configure tools hermes gateway # start messaging gateway

The setup wizard walks you through choosing a provider, configuring API keys, enabling tools, and connecting messaging platforms. It's not as hand-holding as OpenClaw's openclaw onboard wizard, but it covers everything you need.

Coming from OpenClaw?

Hermes has a built-in migration tool:

hermes claw migrate # Full interactive migration hermes claw migrate --dry-run # Preview what would be migrated hermes claw migrate --preset user-data # Migrate without secrets

This imports your SOUL.md, memories, skills, API keys, channel configs, and TTS assets. The migration is designed to move user data without carrying over secrets.

The Learning Loop: How Hermes Actually Gets Smarter

This is the feature that sets Hermes apart from every other agent. Let me break down each component and how it works in practice.

1. Persistent Memory with Periodic Nudges

Hermes maintains two memory stores:

  • MEMORY.md — the agent's own notes about the environment, tool quirks, project conventions, and lessons learned. Think of it as the agent's personal knowledge base. USER.md — a profile of who you are: communication preferences, coding style, recurring corrections, timezone, role. This is what makes the agent feel personalized.

The key detail: Hermes nudges itself to persist knowledge. After a session where you correct its approach or share a preference, the agent proactively saves it. You don't have to explicitly say "remember this." The next session, that knowledge is already loaded into context.

Example: After I corrected Hermes three times about using Chinese for communication, it saved a memory entry: "Communication language: always use Chinese." Now every new session starts in Chinese without prompting.

2. Automatic Skill Creation

After any complex task — defined as 5+ tool calls with reasoning between them — Hermes autonomously creates a skill. Skills are procedural memory: reusable step-by-step approaches for recurring task types.

Each skill is a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter (name, tags, version) and markdown body (trigger conditions, numbered steps, pitfalls, verification steps). They live in ~/.hermes/skills/.

Example: After a debugging session involving SSH tunnel setup and port forwarding, Hermes created a ssh-tunnel-debug skill. Next time I hit a similar issue, the skill fires automatically — with the exact commands and common pitfalls already documented.

3. Skill Self-Improvement

Skills aren't static. When Hermes uses a skill and encounters a step that's outdated, incomplete, or wrong, it patches the skill immediately. This means skills get better with use — they accumulate pitfalls, edge cases, and shortcuts that the initial creation couldn't anticipate.

This happens in practice: a skill that originally had 5 steps grows to 12 steps after a week of use, accumulating platform-specific workarounds, error handling, and verification steps nobody would have thought to document up front.

4. FTS5 Session Search

Hermes stores every conversation in a local SQLite database with FTS5 full-text search. When it encounters a new problem, it can search its own past conversations for relevant context — across sessions.

This means if you solved a similar problem three months ago, Hermes can find that conversation and apply the same approach. No other mainstream agent does this. OpenClaw has session history but no cross-session semantic recall. Claude Code and Codex treat every session as independent.

5. Honcho Dialectic User Modeling

Hermes integrates with Honcho, a dialectic user modeling system. This goes beyond simple preference storage — it builds a progressively deeper model of who you are: how you think, what you prioritize, how you communicate, what frustrates you.

In practice, this means Hermes adapts its communication style over time. If you prefer concise bullet-point answers, it learns to stop writing paragraphs. If you always ask follow-up questions about edge cases, it starts preemptively addressing them. The adaptation is gradual but noticeable after a few weeks.

Key Features

Multi-Platform Messaging

Hermes connects to 6 messaging platforms via its gateway: Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, and Email. You run hermes gateway setup to configure channels, then hermes gateway start to launch the gateway process. All platforms share conversation continuity — start a thread on Telegram, continue on Discord, and the agent remembers the full context.

This is fewer platforms than OpenClaw (24), but it covers the platforms that matter for most developers. The gateway also supports voice memo transcription — send a voice message on Telegram and Hermes transcribes and responds.

Terminal Interface

Hermes has a proper TUI (Terminal User Interface) with multiline editing, slash-command autocomplete, conversation history, interrupt-and-redirect, and streaming tool output. It's built with Python's Ink-inspired framework and feels like a modern terminal app, not a glorified REPL.

Key slash commands shared across CLI and messaging:

Action CLI Messaging
Start fresh /new or /reset /new or /reset
Change model /model provider:model /model provider:model
Set personality /personality name /personality name
Retry/undo /retry, /undo /retry, /undo
Compress context /compress /compress
Browse skills /skills /skill-name
Interrupt work Ctrl+C or new message /stop or new message

```` ````

`

### Model Flexibility

Hermes supports more LLM providers than any other agent I've used:

- Nous Portal — Nous Research's own endpoint
- OpenRouter — 200+ models via a single API
- NovitaAI — AI-native cloud for model API, agent sandbox, and GPU
- NVIDIA NIM — Nemotron models
- Xiaomi MiMo — Chinese LLM provider
- z.ai/GLM — Zhipu AI's GLM models
- Kimi/Moonshot — Moonshot AI
- MiniMax — MiniMax models
- Hugging Face — Open models
- OpenAI, Anthropic, Google — The big three
Custom endpoints — Any OpenAI-compatible API

Switch models instantly with `hermes model` or `/model`. Set different models per scheduled cron job. This is genuinely useful — I run cheap models for routine cron tasks and premium models for complex research.

### Subagent Delegation

Hermes can spawn isolated subagents for parallel workstreams. You describe the goal, provide context, and the subagent runs in its own conversation with its own terminal session. Only the final summary comes back — intermediate tool results never pollute your context window.

Two modes:

- Single task — one subagent, one goal
Batch parallel — up to 3 subagents running concurrently

Example: "Research OpenClaw's latest features, write a comparison table with Hermes, and test the cron scheduler" — Hermes spawns three workers, runs them in parallel, and returns consolidated results.

### Cron Scheduling

Hermes has the most capable cron system of any personal AI agent:

- Natural language descriptions — describe the task in plain English, not cron syntax
- Delivery to any platform — cron output can go to Telegram, Discord, Slack, or any connected channel
- Per-job model override — use a cheap model for daily reports, premium for weekly analysis
- Script-only mode — skip the LLM entirely for simple watchdog tasks
Context chaining — pipe output from one cron job into the next

Example cron job: "Every morning at 8am, check Hacker News top 10, summarize the most interesting AI/developer stories, and send a briefing to my Telegram." No special syntax — just describe what you want.

### 7 Terminal Backends

Hermes can run commands through 7 different backends:

| Backend | Use Case | Idle Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Local | Development, personal machine | Free (your machine) |
| Docker | Isolated execution | Free |
| SSH | Remote server access | Server cost |
| Singularity | HPC environments | Free |
| Modal | Serverless with persistence | Near-zero when idle |
| Daytona | Serverless dev environments | Near-zero when idle |
| Vercel Sandbox | Ephemeral execution | Free tier available |

The Modal and Daytona backends are the standout feature for cost-conscious users. Your agent's environment hibernates when idle and wakes on demand. For someone like me who uses the agent intermittently throughout the day, this means paying for compute only during active sessions — often under $2/month.

### MCP Integration

Hermes has a native MCP (Model Context Protocol) client. Configure servers in `config.yaml` and Hermes automatically discovers and registers their tools. This extends Hermes' capabilities without writing any code — connect any MCP-compatible server for database access, API integrations, or custom tools.

## What I Actually Used It For (3-Week Test)

### Week 1: Setup & Basics

Installation is quick. The setup wizard handles provider selection, tool configuration, and Telegram gateway connection, and you can be chatting with the agent from both Telegram and the terminal on day one.

Key observation: the TUI felt unfamiliar at first (I'm used to simpler CLI tools), but after two days, the slash-command autocomplete and streaming tool output became second nature. The `/compress` command is essential — when context gets long, compress it instead of starting over.

### Week 2: Skills & Memory

This is where Hermes started differentiating itself. After writing two articles with Hermes (each involving web research, drafting, and WordPress publishing), the agent had created 4 skills automatically: `web-research`, `article-drafting`, `wp-cli-publish`, and `seo-optimization`.

The third article went noticeably faster. Hermes remembered my article structure preferences, knew the WordPress CLI commands without looking them up, and preemptively set Rank Math SEO metadata because the skill had been patched to include that step after my first article.

Within a couple of weeks, USER.md accumulates entries about your preferences. Conversations get shorter because the agent starts preemptively doing things you previously had to ask for.

### Week 3: Delegation & Automation

Three cron jobs cover most of the routine value:

- Daily briefing — 8am, top 5 Hacker News stories + weather → Telegram
- Server monitoring — every 30min, check disk/memory/CPU → alert if above 80%
Weekly summary — Monday 9am, summarize all tasks completed that week → Discord

All three run reliably. The daily briefing improves as the agent accumulates context about your interests, and server monitoring catches disk space issues before they become outages.

Subagent delegation is worth testing against a real research task: "Find the top 5 alternatives to Vercel for serverless deployment, compare pricing, and create a summary table." Hermes spawns parallel subagents — one for pricing data, one for feature comparison, one for community sentiment — and returns a consolidated answer in a couple of minutes.

## Where Hermes Falls Short

### 1. Channel Coverage

6 platforms vs OpenClaw's 24. No WhatsApp native integration yet (it's listed but still early), no WeChat, no iMessage, no Microsoft Teams, no Matrix. If you need your agent on those channels, you'll need OpenClaw as a complement — or wait for Hermes to add them.

### 2. No GUI Onboarding

The TUI is powerful but has a learning curve. OpenClaw's `openclaw onboard` wizard is more accessible for non-technical users. Hermes' `hermes setup` covers the same ground but requires comfort with a terminal interface.

### 3. Documentation Gaps

The docs are good for core features but thin on advanced configuration. Understanding cron job delivery targets generally requires reading the source code. The Chinese translation of the README is a nice touch, but the full docs aren't translated.

### 4. Python Runtime Overhead

Compared to ZeroClaw's Rust core, Hermes' Python runtime has higher memory usage and slower cold starts. On a 512MB VPS, you'll feel it. The serverless backends (Modal/Daytona) mitigate this, but local execution on constrained hardware is not Hermes' strength.

### 5. Community Size

158K stars is huge, but OpenClaw's 373K means more contributors, more skills, more bug reports getting filed, and more edge cases getting found. Hermes' community is growing fast (9,000+ commits, 4,200+ issues) but it's still the smaller ecosystem.

## Pricing

Hermes Agent is free and open-source (MIT license). Your only costs are:

- LLM API calls — depends on your provider and model. OpenRouter starts at ~$0.10/1M tokens for budget models, ~$3/1M tokens for flagship models.
- Hosting — $5/month VPS for self-hosting, or near-zero with Modal/Daytona serverless backends.
Messaging platform costs — Telegram/Discord/Slack bots are free. WhatsApp Business API has its own costs.

Total cost depends entirely on the models you route to. Running OpenRouter lets you mix budget models for routine work with premium models for the hard problems, and because every request is metered per token you can attribute spend to research, article writing, cron jobs and delegation separately. Set a monthly cap in the provider dashboard before you start — an agent that delegates will find ways to spend it.

global_articles.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
global_articles.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.
